This is a most unusual resolution-
I was referring to the resolution favouring the raising of the indemnity of members of parliament.
-as I believe most people think the members of parliament are already overpaid. The situation has been a little difficult during tbe past few years because of the high income tax and the necessity of a member having to maintain two homes. If some consideration wrere given the expenses incurred while in Ottawa personally I do not consider the present indemnity too low.
About seventy-five per cent of the wage earners in Canada receive less than $1,000 per year, so a member of parliament with $4,000 is in the high income bracket. The thing we should set our mind to is to increase the national income so that there could Ibe an increase in the income levels all round. Until that is done, I could not feel justified in arguing for a higher indemnity for members of parliament.
We have asked our young men to make great sacrifices even the sacrifice of life itself during the past few years. I do not believe that

That was my position then; it is my position now. The thing I object to in regard to this increase in members' indemnities is that it is being camouflaged as an allowance, and an allowance that is free from income tax. It is a fifty per cent increase in the indemnities of the members, and nothing less; but worse than that, it is proposed to make it free of income fax while we are still collecting income tax from incomes as low as $660 for a single person [DOT]and $1,200 for a married person. In my opinion nothing parliament could do would be more damaging to itself than to pass the bill now before us. Let me put the case in this' way. When we were children we were told about the conduct expected of the officers of a ship overtaken by disaster at sea. The safety of the women and children, those weakest and most helpless, is considered the first responsibility of the ship's officers and crew. They are helped into the lifeboats first; then, if there is time, the crew, the< officers and last of all the captain are saved. How different is the procedure we are asked to adopt here. The captain of the ship of state tells us that it is more important to save the officers than the passengers; more important, in times of rising unemployment and increased living costs, to see to it that members of parliament are put beyond the fear of insecurity and want, than to see that those existing on the miserable pittance of the old age pension or on lower wage scales are put in a position where they can at least keep their heads above water. I was wondering also what the hon. member's logic would be if he felt that it was his vote that would decide whether this would be paid. He might act just the same, but it would be interesting to know.
Enough of that. I rose to say that I commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for keeping his word, and I support him in this move because I feel it is one that has been delayed too long. My judgment is that the members of this house are no less important to Canada than are the congressmen of the United States. I think it is well known that the congressmen of the United States are given an allowance of $10,000, plus an additional amount up to $10,000 for assistance in carrying on their work during the year. I have said on another occasion that one of the disabilities that the ordinary members of this house suffer is that they have little if any secretarial assistance to prepare the voluminous material necessary in studying the various matters that come before this house. They have to dig out the material themselves; they have to spend their own time and often their own money in getting material. If a member does his duty in this house he has very little if any opportunity outside of the period he is in Ottawa to do anything but prepare himself for the work and the duties of this assembly.
Six thousand dollars is not a very handsome sum to people who give their whole attention to the business of such an assembly as this, and who serve their constituencies. In supporting the Prime Minister's motion I have in mind the improvement in the democratic procedure in Canada. I have always taken the position that a member should visit his constituency at least twice a year. He should go to his people before the session to get their instructions. That is the only way in which the- people can control the members of this house and get their will. To do that requires considerable money and considerable time. I think it is the duty of every member after a session of the House of Commons to visit his constituency and make a report

not just in one centre, but to go to the people and get their approval, we will say, of the things he has done. During the time I represented people in the legislature of Alberta I made it a point to cover my constituency twice each year. I visited every centre in the constituency and that is what I propose to do in the large Peace River constituency that I now represent. It would be impossible to do that on the indemnity that was set at $4,000.

Senate and Home of Commons
Just one point further. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) contended that the passage of this measure would create a special class of citizen which was not taxed. That is not so. The income tax act of this country makes provision for deduction from taxable income of certain sums of money spent in earning the income as necessary expenses. This applies to travelling salesmen or railroad workers, such as engineers, firemen and brakemen. Many, of these men must maintain more than one domicile. They have their family domicile, and at the end of the line where they may have to spend a day or two they have another. They are allowed deductions from their taxable income to cover expenses paid in earning the income.
I have taken the position on more than one occasion that this privilege ought to be extended to the members of this house. No one, can deny that hon. members certainly spend a large portion of their indemnity of $4,000 in earning it, and they always have done so. Under the circumstances I must deny completely that it would be creating a special class in this country. It is merely extending to the members of parliament a principle that has been extended already to a large number of citizens engaged in other pursuits. Under the circumstances I must give my support to the measure.

Mr. Speaker, when the Prime
Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made a statement by way of introducing the second reading of this bill, he outlined briefly what he regarded as its principle. He stated that it was to provide $2,000 to meet the expenses of members of parliament, and that in addition it provided for a deduction from that item for non-attendance at this house, and provided also that that increased indemnity should be taxable when paid to members of the other place, to members of the cabinet, and to the leader of the opposition. I think that is a correct statement of the principle of this measure.
As I see it, the bill before us proposes, first, an increase in the indemnities of private members of the House of Commons of $2,000 that increase not to be taxed; second, an increase in the indemnities of the members of the other place, that increase to be subject to taxation; third, an increase in the indemnity paid to members of the cabinet and the leader of the opposition, that increase to be taxable.
The bill is based on a resolution which superseded a resolution introduced in this house 'some time ago, and for certain aspects of that change I commend the government. I could not have opposed the proposal to increase the indemnities of the private mem-

bers of this house, but I could not have supported the proposal to increase the indemnities of the cabinet and the leader of the opposition without requiring that they be taxable. So I commend the government for this feature o'f its change in policy.	.
The question now before this house is whether the proposal is or is not a good one for this country. I suggest that the answer depends upon the point mentioned by the Prime Minister, namely, whether it is going to improve the contribution which members of parliament can make to this nation from this time forward. I am not going to take time to-day to discuss that. I wish to comment upon one thing, the question of what this measure means. I think there has been a wrong interpretation in several respects of what it does mean.
I understand that the last adjustment of indemnities was some twenty-five years ago. Since that time what has happened? The income of the Canadian people has doubled. v The average wage and salary increases in ten of the leading industries of this country amount to one-third. Meanwhile, the time required of members of both houses in the pursuance of their duties has increased.
One thing which I think has always been wrong in connection with this matter is that the expenses of members of both houses have not been allowed as a deductible item in the income tax return. That, it seems to me, is the chief argument in favour of an adjustment of this kind at this time. Business people have it. Members of parliament should not be denied it.
I have had a rough calculation made to try to see exactly what the proposals in this bill mean, because they do not mean a net increase of S2,000 except to the private members of the House of Commons. The calculation I have here was made on the basis of an income tax payer *with only one dependent, his wife, and no dependent children. The net income of a member of this house or the other from his indemnity in 1938 after paying income tax was §3,930; in 1944, a typical year during the war, it was $3,036; a reduction of $900.
Is that for a married man or a single man?

A married man with no dependents other than his wife. Should this measure go through, his income after paying the tax would be $5,190, or an increase of $1,260 over his pre-war net income from this source; that is, about a one-third increase.


:

In the case of members of the other place the figures for the first two years are the same -1938, $3,930; 1944, $3,036. If this bill goes through, assuming they have no other income -which perhaps is not a correct assumption- their net income after paying the tax will be $4,475, an increase of $545 over pre-war.
But the interesting thing in this calculation is more with respect to the members of the cabinet and the leader of the opposition. Assuming they have no other income, their net income in 1938 would have been $12,980, and in 1944, $7,741, a reduction of five thousand dollars. That is the burden the members of the cabinet have been carrying during these years, and even with this adjustment now, it will bring their net income to $9,617, which represents a reduction of $3,300 in comparison with pre-war income from this source-a twenty-five per cent reduction even after this increase in indemnity is made.	-
I am not arguing on one side or the other in this matter at the present time. I have been trying to analyse the situation. I do not mind saying that personally this question is a bit embarrassing to me. I have been wondering what position to take, what position would be proper, and. I have come to a conclusion, which I will summarize in a moment. But the question before us is this: What are we going to do? Here is this measure. We must support it or oppose it. I could criticize it in some respects. I could criticize it as being untimely. Members of this house to-day are not worth fifty per cent more than they were a year ago; but they were worth more a year ago than they got.
It may be untimely too in that there are other inequities that have not been corrected in this nation. The member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) has raised that point and he says he hesitates to approve this measure while other inequities remain uncorrected. For such measures as this government has taken to correct those inequities it deserves credit. For such omissions as it has been guilty of in not having corrected those inequities it must accept censure, and I shall be one-I believe there are many others-who will censure it for those things. But the question is, shall we deny a measure of justice simply because there are other inequities that have not been corrected?
As for myself, and every other member for that matter, we cannot blow hot and cold at the same time on the measure. We have either to accept it or to reject it. Personally I should prefer to have nothing to do with it. I have considered whether we should move an amendment. I have considered whether I should
34S9

Senate and House of Commons
refuse to accept it myself. Briefly, this is my position. I think I should look like a piker trying to get some measure of public acclaim by opposing a bill which in some quarters will be unpopular. As I have said, the bill gives some degree of justice to private members of this house, even though I think it is untimely, and even though I am sure there are other inequities that call for correction in Canada at this time. Under all the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, this measure will receive no opposition from me, nor, I hope, will it receive opposition from any large section of the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In view of the statements we have heard this morning from leaders of the several parties opposite, and in the light of what I said yesterday, I might possibly be expected to allow the matter to rest there. However, I feel that some statements have been made which ought to be considered a little further and I therefore propose to add to what has already been said on this question.
First, may I remind hon. members that there are 245 members in the house and of that number only three private members have spoken on the measure, of whom two have opposed it, the other having supported it. All the leaders of the different parties in the ^iouse have supported the measure and have given substantial reasons for doing so, reasons which are all related to the public interest. I wish to thank hon. gentlemen who lead the several parties for joining with me in helping to make clear to the country the reasons which actuate the govemqient and parliament in taking this step at this time.
As regards the suggestion that its introduction at this time is "untimely", I do not agree with that at all. I think its introduction at this session is timely, and very timely. It is never too late to remedy a wrong or an injustice so long as that is possible, and personally I think the time has long since passed when this parliament should have had more consideration for those who are sent here by the people" as their representatives to serve the country' in the making of its laws and in protecting the financial, human and other resources of the nation. I say that it is better to do something, albeit late, than never at all. The measure is either right in

Senate and House of Commons
itself or it is not. If it is right in itself, it is timely, and I for one am quite prepared to say that it is most timely at this particular moment.
That brings me to say a few words to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) who has been, with one exception, the only one that has been critical of this measure. First of all may I say to him and to the house that he and I have known each other for a long time, and that like all who know him I think we will agree as to his sincerity and deep convictions, and I would hope that no one would question those in any particular. But may I say to my hon. friend that he too knows us, that when he talks about convictions he ought to be prepared to attribute to all other hon. members the same motives and the same convictions as he is crediting himself with. That he did not do. I was sorry when I heard him say that when it came to a choice between conviction and comfort that he preferred conviction. I think on reflection my hon. friend will regret that he made that remark. So far as I am concerned I propose to deal with him and with other hon. members in precisely the same way, namely, in the belief that each in his action at this time either in supporting this measure by word openly in the House of Commons, or in giving acquiescence in silence, is acting from honourable motives and profound conviction.
My hon. friend said this morning that I had mentioned yesterday that one of the purposes of the increased allowance to members was to attract the best type of member to parliament. He then looked over the House of Commons and said that he thought we had here the best house that had existed for some time. I agree with him in that. I believe the calibre of members of this house is as high as, if not higher than, that of any House of Commons in any of the other parliament of Canada. But may I say that that does not mean that we might not have had in this parliament to-day many other hon. members who would have been ih an exceptional position to give of the benefit of their wide experience to the country at this time if before the last election took place there had been something more in the way of an allowance to members of parliament. I know of my own personal experience that I tried my best, but tried in vain, to have certain members of my own party who had served in parliament and who had had wide experience in public affairs to run again. I could not get them to run, not because they expected they would be defeated-they would have been elected beyoDd any doubt-but

for the reason that they felt, knowing what thear expenses had become, what it had cost them in their personal obligations, in their businesses or practice or the like, they could not afford in these circumstances to come back into parliament. I know what I am saying now is also true of the membership of other parties in this house. I know that their leaders have sought to get outstanding men, men of wide experience, to come into parliament, and they have met with exactly the same kind of situation as I was faced with myself.
May I say further that I know that there are members in this house to-day who came in with the belief that there was going to be an increased allowance and who are finding the situation very trying at the present time. Unless they do secure something more in the way of allowance some of them may be tempted to resign, thereby occasioning byelections in the country. That is known to many hon. members, and it ought to be known to the country.
When my hon. friend says that members [DOT]here expected to get only the same allowance as was given in the last parliament, he is not stating the situation correctly. I made an important statement in the last parliament, and repeated it during the election campaign, that if the present government were returned I would be among the first to support an increase in the indemnity of members, that if I were not in this House of Commons, I would support it anyway. Many of those who are in this house to-day accepted that statement at its face value, and came into the house expecting when they were here they would not have to serve with the allowance what it was before, but would receive an increased allowance.
Perhaps it might be as well if I were to read at once what I said in the last session of the last parliament so that no hon. member can say that I am overstating what I said or that I have in any way changed my attitude. I believe what I said at the time will go a long way toward answering much of what has been said by the two members who spoke in opposition to this measure this morning. My remarks will be found in Hansard of August 14, 1944, at page 6499. As I recall my remarks were made in the morning during the course of a debate on a number of financial matters. I said:
I cannot say whether I shall be in this House of Commons in another parliament, but if I am I will certainly be prepared to agree with lion, members who deem it advisable that in the interests of the membership of the House of Commons, the indemnity should be regarded strictly as an indemnity and not as a salary, and, therefore, not be liable to taxation.

Senate and House oj Commons
That statement was before this country in the last election. I was speaking then as a leader of a political party-the Liberal party- and if the people of the country had been opposed to the idea of an allowance to members being regarded as an indemnity and not taxable we would have heard about it on the platforms from one end of this country to the other. An effort would have been made to defeat myself and my party on that ground. I ask any hon. member in this house, did he hear any question of the kind raised by the electors in this country? I did not. I heard no opposition whatever to it, nor did they.
Just the other way round.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I continue:
I believe that the independence of parliament and the independence of the members of the House of Commons is something that we must seek to maintain at all costs. I regard the amount voted as an indemnity as something intended by parliament to help secure that independence. I have before me a copy of the debate in the British House of Commons on August 10, 1911, when a statement was made by the Prime Minister of that day that at the session following the general election he would arrange for members to be paid. I should like to quote what Mr. Lloyd George, who was chancellor of the exchequer at the time, had to say in reference thereto. I shall quote his words later, but in effect he said that he believed that the House of Commons should be as representative as possible of all classes in the community, not representative merely of certain classes. He said that the British House of Commons, as then constituted was made up in a large part of those who came from the learned professions or who were wealthy: he felt that the house should be more broadly representative, that it should have members returned in larger numbers from the working classes, as they are sometimes termed, from the agricultural communities, that there should be as members more persons of talent and ability though in humble circumstances financially.
I feel strongly that at this time of all times-
And may I say there in reference to the timeliness of the present bill that I made this statement last session before the general election. I was not afraid of the timeliness because there were some difficult problems to settle in the country, because some people were not as fortunate as others. I was stating then what I thought was timely at the time, and which I believe is even more timely to-day. I continue:
I feel strongly that at this time of all times we should seek to obtain .the best possible representation in the House of Commons of Canada and have it broadened by having as many elements of the community represented as it is possible to have.
I was taking a step then, appealing to the electorate itself, if you wish to put it that way, because that is what it is when a man
speaks as a leader in parliament. I was appealing to the people to find ways and means whereby we could get the best type of man in this country to serve in its halls of parliament. Knowing the circumstances of our day, the electors would appreciate very quickly what was involved. I continue:
The other evening I expressed the hope that, in a subsequent parliament, there would be not merely business and professional men, but members chosen from among those who are in the fighting forces to-day as well as a larger representation of labour, a larger rural representation and a larger representation of women, and representatives from no particular class but chosen because of their special gifts, talents and high character. To make that possible in times like the present-
There again is your "timely" reference.
-it will be necessary that those who are chosen as candidates shall feel that they will be in a position to exercise their duties in this House of Commons in a perfectly independent way, without fear and without favour. What was found in Britain when labour began to be represented in the house was that a string was tied to its representation; members came in as members of the .labour party, but they were bound in advance to support only certain measures. They were not free agents representing the country as a whole, or even their constituencies as a whole, but representing a class. Nothing could be worse than that we should have in this country a membership composed of those who represent classes, whatever those classes may be. A member of parliament represents the people of the nation at large, all classes. The danger is this, that unless there is an indemnity that is sufficiently large to ensure independence on the part of members we are going to have this House of Commons composed increasingly of those who are so independent in means of their own, or because of their associations with powerful interests. that they will come to constitute, as compared with others, a very large section of the membership of the house. In other words, we shall have a privileged class here at a time when the world is doing the best it can-in perhaps the worst possible way-to get rid of a lot of privilege and to recognize that there is a certain equality in men regardless of the particular class to which they may belong, or their particular calling.
I would recommend those words to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. IJerridge), who has spoken about the danger of establishing a privileged class here. If he reads over my remarks I think he will find1 that I have answered him on the point of creating privilege.
There is another danger, and that is that we shall have men elected to this House of Commons who, through the inability to secure a different type of candidate, would not be able to earn an income outside of parliament comparable with that which would be secured to them by an indemnity, or coming here, may I say, under obligation, some of them, to corporations, others to special interests, but not free agents.

private and personal interests; or does he mean himself as one who has been sent to parliament to speak for the people of Canada, and that in regard to any matter which may come up? If he wishes to preserve his independent-
Mr. MaeINNIS: The Prime Minister is asking me a question and, if he wishes me to answer it, I will do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Very well,
Proceed.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I have listened to a great many discussions on this matter.

Answer, then.
Mr. MaeINNIS: But I have never heard it discussed except from the personal point of view of the member. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) asked a minute ago what my logic would be if I had-
Don't make a speech.

Oh, oh.
Mr. MaeINNIS: Well, that is the answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. member has only helped to emphasize his position, a position to which I am taking exception. He claims he is speaking as a person, and in relation to his own views as a person, his own affairs. I say every hon. member has to consider himself in two relationships, one as an individual who if he is to live has to earn an income, who has to support a family-if he is fortunate enough to have one-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And I say that designedly. I want hon. members to see that I am not thinking about myself at the present time. *
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have very great sympathy for men who have families of sixteen or seventeen, like some of my friends here, but who nevertheless come to serve as members of the House of Commons. And may I say the House of Commons is all the better for having them here, those with large families, because they can speak with added' authority on these questions. But the point I was seeking to emphasize is that when we speak of ourselves we have to make clear that distinction. Let me ask hon. members this question: If the men, and- the lady, who are in this chamber to-day were thinking only of themselves as individuals, and were not thinking rather of themselves as representatives of the people in parliament, how many of them would be
Senate and House of Commons

giving up what they are obliged to give up when they come to the House of Commons, which necessitates their being away from their homes, their businesses and their professions?
In large part the House of 'Commons is composed of hon. members who have important business interests and' connections, who hold* important positions in their professions and several avocations

andi who, may I say, have not infrequently been chosen by the electorate for that very reason. Do Hot forget that. Members of the House of Commons are representing people who know them; and it is amongst other reasons because their constituents believe that their member is a person who will be prepared to make sacrifices for the public good, and because they believe he understands public questions that he is sent here. I say if those members stopped and said to themselves, "Would I be richer or better off at the end of the year if I stayed at home and attended to my practice as a physician or my profession as a lawyer, or if I attended to my 'business or calling, be it what it may, instead of being a member of parliament?" the answer would be that a large percentage of members of the House of Commons would not be here to-day-and the loss would be great to the nation.
This is a distinction I wish to make clear when the hon. member asks about our looking after ourselves. I say to him that in this matter of indemnities we should not be thinking about ourselves at all as individuals who have personal obligations. We should be thinking of ourselves primarily as members of parliament, as trustees of the nation, as persons shouldering the responsibility of spending billions of dollars of the country's money, and as persons who are anxious to place ourselves in a position where, whether we deal with questions affecting the rich, the poor, or any other class, we can speak our minds without fear and without favour.
I now come to another statement the hon. member made, and one which I believe ought to be cleared up. The hon. member said that we are not granting relief to others, and that it was colossal impudence for the government to bring forward this measure at the present time when nothing was being done for those who were in ^traitened circumstances. I say it is colossal impudence on the part of the hon. member to make a statement of the kind. Not only is it colossal impudence to address the government in those terms, but it is colossal impudence to impute to the House of Commons and to parliament the suggestion that parliament has been doing nothing to relieve distress during the time it has been here.
[Mr. Mackenzie KLu^.J
I ask the hon. member if the greater part [DOT] of this session has not been devoted to considering1 ways and means whereby we can prevent-in addition to the necessity of relieving those of whom he has spoken-hundreds of thousands of people from getting into a position where they will require relief at all. The whole effort of parliament in supporting the government's policies has been to maintain a high level of employment, to maintain a national income of larger proportions, in order that we may not have to be seeking ways and means of relieving persons by the thousands, if not by the hundreds of thousands.
When we consider the policies that have been put forward, policies which have helped create in many countries throughout the world a demand for our goods, policies which have been giving employment which would not otherwise have existed; when one thinks of what has been done for families by distributing to every home where there is young children means whereby they will not feel the distress which otherwise they would feel; when one thinks of what parliament has done in preventing inflation; I say that when one considers these policies, apart from many others, one will see at once that the hon, member is wrong in what he says. I am not crediting the government with this; I am saying that that is what the parliament of Canada has done-and it was the parliament of Canada about which my hon. friend was talking when he spoke in terms of "colossal impudence". I say parliament has recognized its great obligation to the nation, and has recognized it in a magnificent way-and I am speaking irrespective of any party in the house, and giving credit to every representative in the two houses of parliament.
Perhaps I have spoken at sufficient length. Let me say this, however: When the hon. member says that this measure is camouflage, then I think he had better give second thought to that expression. I am not camouflaging in the words I am using, but when I saw my hon. friend having to read much of his speech, and look to his notes to give a list of the difficulties that he said people were experiencing, a lack of this and a lack of that, then refer to his papers to see what else he could bring up that would help to raise prejudice in the minds of many in this country, I began to think there was some camouflage in the speech which he had made.
May I say this one word in conclusion. My hon. friend has said that, the men who come into this parliament would be better members if they themselves had suffered from privation or poverty. I take no issue with him on that whatever, provided that they come in

Senate and House of Commons
with the wisdom that ought to be bom of an experience of the kind, without bitterness or prejudice, and prepared thereby to help to make things better for others. But I ask myself: Is the desire to help others the monopoly of the very few? What is the motive that has brought into parliament ninety per cent, if not ninety-nine per cent, of the members that are in this house to-day. There doubtless are exceptions, but I would say that the motive above every other was a desire to help their fellow men and improve conditions for the great body of people in the country. I believe that with most men who go into public life that is the actuating motive, and I do not care whether a member is as well to do as Crcesus, or as poor as a mouse-
A church mouse.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend says "church mouse". I do believe that the motive in the hearts of most men here, men whose families*have been willing to have them leave their homes to go to serve their country in parliament, is that they may help to improve conditions for others.
Somewhere along the path of life sacrifice has played its part in the making of men. I have been fortunate in having had parents who made sacrifices for me. I would not be here to-day; I would not be in public life today except for the sacrifices of' others. This has made it possible for me to take the part I have taken in public life. I do not forget that before my parents, there were others of theirs who had experienced terrific hardships in seeking to defend freedom and the liberties of the people and to improve the lot of the great masses of the people. I believe it is true that there is not a member of this house who when he looks back into the past will not find that in his early days he has suffered something in the way of privation or distress or that those before him of his own had not known privation and in whose heart there is not as a consequence a desire to improve things for others. Love for and a readiness to help the poor is not a monopoly of a chosen few. We all come by it in one way or another. My mother's father, who himself had suffered exile and imprisonment for causes in which he believed, once said, speaking of the early experiences of his life:
Well may I love the poor, greatly may I esteem the humble and the lowly, for poverty and adversity were my nurses, and in youth were want and misery my familiar friends; even now it yields a sweet satisfaction .to my soul, that I can claim kindred with the obscure cottar, and the humble labourer, of my native, ever honoured ever loved Scotland.
Those words have gone deeply into my soul, more so than any other words I have ever heard or read. I have tried to be true to the trust they have imposed on me. In them will be found the motive which has kept me in public life and I believe a kindred motive has, to a greater or less extent, helped to bring into public life every man and woman in this house.

speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the senate to bill No. 15, to confer certain transitional powers upon the governor in council during the national emergency arising out of the war.
He said: There were two amendments made to the emergency powers bill in the senate. One of them is a decided clarification whioh

will be valuable in the interpretation of the . act. It is to add at the end of the act the following:
In this act "war with Germany and Japan" means the war that commenced on the tenth day of September, 1939, against the German reich and subsequently against Italy, Finland, Hungary, Roumania and Japan.
This is for the purpose of making it apparent that when we speak of "the end of the war with Germany and Japan" we mean the end of the war with all those who were allied with them over the past years.'
The other amendment, I thought, was not at all necessary but it certainly is not harmful. It is, to insert after the words "orders and regulations" in section 4 and before the words "made under the War Measures Act" the word "lawful". It read1 before:
the orders and regulations made under the War Measures Act or pursuant to authority created under the said act in force immediately before the day this act comes into force shall . . . continue in full force-	'
It was felt that there might be some suggestion that this was validating things which had not been lawfully made. My view was that if they had not been lawfully made they were not in force, because when the question goes before the courts, it is not to annul an order but it is to get a declaration that it never was validly made and therefore has no possible legal operation. But the insertion of the word "lawfully" cannot make any embarrassing. change. Now it will read "orders and regulations lawfully made under the War Measures Act".
I think that this house could very well accept the amendments which have thus "been made.

I believe there should be more careful investigation into this act than it has already had. Since we were last considering the bill in this house it has been in the hands of the banking and commerce committee where members have been examining two witnesses, namely, Mr. Rasminsky and to some extent Mr. Mackintosh.
A good deal of information was elicited in the committee, as a result of the consideration of which I think we shall probably be able to judge better what attitude we should take with respect to the bill.
One important thing has occurred since we were discussing the matter in the house and in the committee, namely, that the British house has accepted Bretton Woods. Hon. members will recall that I said at one stage in the discussion, in fact at several stages, that the British house was being clubbed into the acceptance of Bretton Woods. More than a few members have taken me to task for having made that statement. I believe that some of the recent pronouncements from Britain will have a bearing on the matter and I wonder therefore if hon. members will bear with me while I read into the record some of the recent utterances on the question.
The radio to-day, I am informed, carries several important statements, for instance:
Churchill asks the Conservatives to refrain from votes, as a heavy vote would hurt British interests in the United States.
This information is contained also in the Ottawa Journal of to-day.
May I examine that statement for a moment or two? Churchill asks the Conservatives to refrain from voting. May I ask hon. members if any one of them supposes that Churchill would have done that had he considered the Bretton Woods agreement to be in the interests of Great Britain, or of the British empire, or of the world? Would anyone suspect Winston Churchill, the great war prime minister, of having played politics to the extent of depriving the world of so great a benefit as some of the advocates of Bretton Woods have tried to make us believe is to be derived from the agreement?
There is another important aspect to that statement. Obviously the Conservatives in Great Britain, if they had voted on the measure, would have voted against the acceptance of Bretton WcSods; for Mr. Churchill says that a heavy vote would have hurt British interests in the United States. Already there was a heavy enough vote. If this house succeeds in rolling up as heavy an adverse vote as the British house did, fifty voting actively against it, this house will do a good deal better than it has thus far shown signs of intending to do. If this house can have relatively as large a proportion of its members refraining from voting for Bretton Woods as refrained from voting in Britain, the results again will be impressive and much more optimistic for those who oppose Bretton Woods than I feel justified in expecting here.
There is another important implication in the statement, namely, that Churchill seems to suspect that in the United States administration there is an attitude which would cause that administration to take steps that would be retaliatory against Great Britain, adversely

affecting the interests of Britain in the United States. As just one common member of this house trying to think his way .through this whole thing, I ask sincerely, in the light of that statement, does anyone suppose that Britain was not clubbed into accepting Bretton Woods?
Right after Mr. Churchill made that remark a foreign minister said that the statement was a libel on the administration of the United States. This remark would tend to indicate that my interpretation of Churchill's statement is correct, namely, that in that statement he definitely implied that a heavy vote would adversely affect Great Britain's interest. By that remark he implied that certain people in the United States administration would take punitive measures against Great Britain's interest in the United States.

The government obviously likes the terms of the agreement no better than anyone else-
That should be interesting to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I continue:
[DOT]-but knt>ws from records of Washington talks that they aTe the best that can be obtained. The Conservatives are not enamoured of them either, but in the absence of any alternative plan to ease the nation's desperate plight, are abstaining from to-night's division so that they will have their hands free to criticize if need be later on.
In the light of that statement we might conclude that they were going to play politics, but in the light of the statement which I have recently read they were not playing politics so much as would be indicated by this statement. I continue:
Some labour members are bitterly opposed to the loan because they think it will hog-tie the socialist programme and they are being left to vote according to their consciences.
Only Lord Beaverbrook has a plan all cut and dried. In his newspapers he is urging rejection of the loan so that Britain can retire into empire free trade-
I feel that the idea in mind there is the Bretton Woods proposals. The article goes on:
-and use the immense internal commerce of the commonwealth as ,a bargaining weapon to exact liberal trading terms from foreign nations -including the United States.
But Bea verb rook's cause is lost. It is not even getting the support of the Conservative party which negotiated the Ottawa agreements of 1932 and placed Britain's trading on a limited imperial preference basis. It is conceded that the Beaverbrook plan would be the only alternative to the American loan. But no party can bring itself to face the bleak prospect of prolongation and probable tightening of austerity living which must result if the loan is rejected.
So, with a feeling that they are signing part of the nation's birthright away, Britain's legislators to-day are accepting the inevitable.
That hardly leaves any doubt as to whether or not Britain is being clubbed into accepting Bretton Woods. I believe that gives real

Bretton Woods Agreements
reason to hon. members for reconsidering the whole question of Bretton Woods and the bill which is based upon it.
May I refer to two or three things which have occurred in this debate and in the country so that we might more successfully examine the bill and the Bretton Woods proposals now before us. In the minister's speech we were told that the issue involved in Bretton Woods, and presumably in the bill based upon it is this:	Shall we have peace? May
I read from the minister's remarks as they appear on page 3040 of Hansard'.
That issue is: are we and other countries to organize and cooperate for peace, or is each nation going to use its strength and resources at the expense of others in a struggle for survival?
We have been told that the principle of this bill, which was given second reading by the house, was international cooperation to prevent us from getting into economic troubles in the future. Just to make sure that I am not misinterpreting, may I read from the words of the Minister of Finance in reply to a statement of the hon. member for Souris, as they appear on page 3218 of Hansard:
Yes. The principle would be international cooperation to prevent us from getting into economic troubles in the future.
Well, apparently Britain does not feel very confident that she is going to keep out of economic troubles through signing the thing, but that is the stand of the Minister of Finance, couched in his own words. The government's reason for supporting this bill T think is to be gathered from the white pape-issued to the house in April, 1945, by the Minister of Reconstruction, on page 7 of which I find these words:
It would outlaw the discriminatory currency practices which turned trade into economic warfare.
This is the guidance and direction we have up to the present time in our study of thi bill and the Bretton Woods proposal.
It seems to me highly desirable that we should define our terms with some accuracy at this point. Just what are the discriminatory practices, and what is economic war? It will be recalled by all hon. members. I believe, that President Wilson made a statement to the effect that military war always resulted from hot commercial rivalry or economic war. Consequently if by any means we could prevent economic war we might hope to rid ourselves of military war. So the statement in the government white paper on the face of it looks rather attractive. Let us see if we can determine for ourselves what economic warfare is and what are these discriminatory practices. May I read from the statement of the Minister
of Finance again, because I thought he gave a good definition of these discriminatory practices at page 3041 of Hansard, referring to the depression:
The result was the stangulation of world trade and the mutual impoverishment of all countries. The characteristic features of world economic relationships before the war were high and discriminatory tariffs, import quotas, export subsidies, depreciated currencies of uncertain value, discriminatory clearing agreements, multiple currency practices.
It would appear, then, that the reason' the government proposes to support Bretton AVoods and is so desperately anxious for us to approve it is that it will render all such things as the minister has mentioned illegal, or at least will tend to eliminate them. Just to bolster up the minister's words, to some extent, by another authority, may I refer to the speech of Henry Morgenthau, Junior, delivered before the delegates to Bretton Woods, which appears on page 9 of the proceedings of the united nations monetary and financial conference, which I obtained from the House of Commons library. Referring to Bretton Woods he said:
This is the alternative to the desperate tactics of the past-competitive currency depreciation, excessive tariff barriers, uneconomic barter deals, multiple currency practices and unnecessary exchange restrictions-by which governments vainly sought to maintain employment and uphold living standards. In the final analysis these tactics only succeeded in contributing to world-wide depression and even war. The international fund agreed upon at Bretton Woods will help remedy this situation.
It will be noticed that Mr. Morgenthau's remarks are not quite so positive and far-reaching as the statement in the government white paper, and are probably just about the same as the remarks of the minister, as to certainty. I am desirous of being completely fair, because here I am endeavouring to conduct a cold-blooded, intellectual inquiry into this whole matter, entirely devoid of passion and strong feeling. AVe have the sort of things that are called trade restrictions. What is economic warfare? May I read to hon. members again the statement in the government white paper, which I fancy is of importance to us because I presume it was written by some of the officials, by Mr. Rasminskv, by Mr. Mackintosh, or perhaps Doctor Clark or perhaps several others. Referring to Bretton Woods it says:
It would outlaw the discriminatory currency practices which turned trade into economic war.
I desire to examine the truthfulness and accuracy of that statement. In order to do so I wish first to get an idea for us to work on as to what economic warfare is and while I do

this I am going to ask hon. members to consider with me the relationships between Canada and the United States to see if we can find out what would constitute economic warfare between these two countries. There must be danger of it. If any hon. member deems that I go astray as I explore this matter I would really appreciate having my attention drawn to the fact. It is well known that Canada has used tariffs for generations. Why does Canada use tariffs against goods coming in from the United States? I think everyone would agree that we use these tariffs for two reasons, first in order to derive revenue therefrom, but perhaps mainly, though I will not be dogmatic on the matter, to keep out of the Canadian market goods from the United States. Canada realizes that if United States shoes, we will say, come into the Canadian market and are sold at a rate below that for which Canadian shoes can be sold, they are the shoes that will be bought and the Canadian product will be left unused; Canadian factories will be in danger of closing and Canadian workmen will be in danger of being thrown out of employment. I wonder if that is right. Then why did Canada raise tariffs against the United States? To protect Canada against United States industrial penetration into Canada. What was that United States industrial penetration? What was the United States doing when she sent goods into Canada to sell for less than the same goods could be produced for here? Was she engaging in economic warfare? If she was not will someone tell me to what extent she was not? If she were allowed to go on sending American goods of all kinds into Canada how long would it be before a vast percentage of the Canadian people would be unemployed, a vast percentage of Canadian wealth would be destroyed, and a vast amount of Canadian revenue would be lost? In other words, economically Canada would be conquered if she did not put up the tariff. May I ask hon. members if any one of them believes that Canada, when she raised the tariff against United States goods coming into Canada, was engaged in economic warfare? Will anyone assert that she was? Hardly. Canada was simply protecting herself against United States economic warfare, was she not?
Let us turn to one of the other trade restric-. tions, namely, foreign exchange control. As is well known, during the war Canada has used foreign exchange control with great wisdom and with great success. What for? It was to prevent too much of United States goods and services from coming into Canada during the war. If I am wrong, will someone tell me. There was a pressure for United States goods
[Mr. Blackmore.l
to enter Canada, even during the war, and if we had not used exchange control and tariffs during the war we would have emerged from it with Canadian industry virtually destroyed. In other words, we should have emerged economically conquered by the United States. Will anyone argue that the foreign exchange control which we exercised during the war was a species of economic warfare? Or, again, was it not a measure designed by Canada for protection from economic warfare?
Let me turn to one further point. In the discussions on this important question I have already referred to what Japan did in 1933 and 1934. She was able to sell for about $5.75 or $6 bicycles for which we would have charged $50 in Canada.
Carried.
No wonder the hon. member feels like calling "carried-", after that. It must be getting pretty hard to stand.
You are right.

Yes, the truth is hard to stand, and especially under these circumstances.
Will anyone argue that Canada should have gone on permitting Japan to sell not only toys and many other things, but bicycles and every other kind of commodity she could produce on a rice standard of living? Would anyone argue that Canada should have allowed those goods to come into this country, thereby displacing Canadian goods and destroying Canadian industry? What did Canada use as a means of preventing any such mishap? She used the quota, did she not, which in effect was an embargo? When Canada used the quota, will anyone argue that she was engag-. ing in economic warfare against Japan? Or was she merely protecting her economy against Japanese economic warfare? I suggest the answer is obvious. She was merely protecting her economy against Japanese economic warfare.
It becomes necessary for Canada from time to time to protect herself against United States economic warfare by means of quotas. There have been times when the United States has endeavoured to dump goods in Canada.
I might refer in that connection to my own constituency, and give an example which hon. members will readily recognize. In the southern part of my constituency strawberries and other small fruits are produced. The growers depend upon the Canadian market. United States growers just across the boundary line, about a hundred miles away, are able to produce the same fruits about two weeks

If we did not do something in the matter United States growers would send their berries into Canada, thereby supplying the Canadian market and filling cellars upon which Canadian producers depend for their market. Obviously that would be a most destructive procedure for Canadian growers. So what do we use? We use anti-dumping laws. What are they? They are a species of quota. Would a Social Credit government impose embargoes against imports of goods? Does the hon. member favour that method of preventing goods from coming in?

I wonder if the hon. member would permit me to answer after I have finished my argument. I shall be happy tc answer it, but just now I am examining the soundness of the government's statement in the white paper that trade restrictions turn trade into economic warfare. I am now asking whether an anti-dumping law, which is a species of quota, was a species of economic warfare, or whether it was a protection against economic warfare from another country. I think all must agree that it was a species of protection against economic warfare.
We have now dealt w'ith three of those undesirable restrictions against trade. Is there any hon. member who would say that he would oppose Canada's use of any of these three restrictions as a means of protecting her economy? I doubt it. And yet apparently Bretton Woods, from the statement of Henry Morgenthau, the statement contained in the Canadian white paper, and the implications which can be drawn from the statement of the Minister of Finance as I have quoted it, is designed to render it less possible to use these protective devices against economic warfare. Would anyone vote for a measure which would render it impossible or less possible for Canada to use these trade restrictions?
It is well known to all hon. members that as soon as the trade balance between Canada and the United States becomes adverse to the extent that Canada is in real danger, the Canadian dollar, if allowed to fluctuate naturally in accordance with the law of supply and demand, will go down in relation to the United States dollar. That is, it will fall in value. What is that fall in value? It is currency depreciation, is it not? It is impossible to get the facts in connection with this matter, but I believe I am correct in saying that the government to-day is deliberately and designedly maintaining the Canadian dollar at a value lower than the United States dollar, largely to keep from having too much
United States goods coming into Canada, and thereby disturbing the Canadian balance of trade position.
Will anyone argue that we should not be free to allow our dollar to fall in value, as compared with the United States dollar, to protect our economy against United States goods? Will anyone argue against the soundness of currency depreciation as a means of protecting our economy against economic warfare with the United States? I doubt very' seriously whether anyone in the committee would do anything that would put Canada in a position in which she could not be free to use currency depreciation, in the event of its being necessary, in order to protect her economy against economic warfare. I do not think any hon. member would venture to say that in allowing that action to be taken Canada would be engaging in economic warfare against the United States. In the light of the four illustrations which I have used, namely, tariffs, foreign exchange control, quotas and currency devaluation; in the light of those four and of the four illustrations, would anyone in this house argue for a moment that Canada in using those four would be engaging in economic warfare?
Take the government's statement in this white paper, which I read once more:
It would outlaw the discriminatory currency practices which turned trade into economic warfare.
It is true that all that is mentioned there is currency practices, and the devaluation of the dollar is only one of those. As I have read in Morgenthau's remarks, and in the minister's remarks in his introductory speech, other trade restrictions are intended; so perhaps I would be justified in reading that statement from the government paper in some such way as this: It would outlaw .the discriminatory currency practices and other trade restrictions which turned trade into economic warfare. If I am doing too much violence to the sense of the statement, the minister will correct me, or Mr. Mackintosh, who I notice is in the chamber ready to assist the minister.
Z I wish to examine that statement in the light of the facts. Will anyone in the light of what I have said argue that trade restrictions such as tariffs, exchange control, depreciation of currency and quotas would turn trade into economic warfare? Would anyone in this chamber accept that for a moment? Is it not rather tfue that economic warfare brings on trade restrictions, tariffs, depreciation of currencies, quotas and exchange controls? From what I have said I think it must be clear that the statement made in the government white paper is an absolute eco-

nomic fallacy. Apparently the government's policy with regard to Bretton Woods is based on an economic fallacy. Apparently that was not by accident, because the passage in the minister's speech to which I referred carries the same idea. May I read it again? He said:
The result was the strangulation of world trade and the mutual impoverishment of all countries. The characteristic features of world . economic relationships before the war were high and discriminatory tariffs, import quotas, export subsidies, depreciated currencies of uncertain value, discriminatory clearing agreements, multiple currency practices.
May I read the words following that statement where the minister continues:
I am certain that in no quarter of the house is there a desire to see the world return to these pre-war practices. But if the nations of the world are left to their own devices and are not bound together in an association of mutual advantage which will set certain standards for its members, they will in my opinion inevitably revert to the practices I have described.
The minister will correct me if I draw a false conclusion. The conclusion I am drawing is that the minister was endeavouring to argue in favour of the adoption of Bretton Woods on the ground that it would prevent these practices. Does anyone in this house wish to see the nations tied to an agreement that will render it impossible for the various nations to use such measures as are at their disposal to protect their economy against economic warfare? We have been told time and again by certain men in this chamber that Canada will derive much benefit from Bretton Woods. I ask hon. members if they think Canada will derive much benefit from an agreement that would render her unable to keep up tariffs to protect her own industries, unable to adopt foreign exchange control in case of need, unable to apply quotas and anti-dumping duties, unable to allow her dollar to fall in relation to her neighbour's dollar; would anyone consider that a measure that prevented her from using those would be a measure in the interest of Canada, that from the application of such a measure Canada would derive any benefit?
Let us leave Canada for a while. Let us remember that Canada is just one of the weaker economies. As a result of her war effort, Britain has become another weaker economy. That is why it is of such desperate seriousness to Britain that the Bretton Woods agreement is forced upon her at the present time. Evident^ Britain understands that when Bretton Woods is applied to her it will be impossible for her to use the tariff to keep out United States goods if she wishes to keep them out. impossible for her to use quotas,

impossible for her to use foreign exchange control, and impossible for her to use depreciation of currency.
Would the hon. member be good enough to read the portions of the Bretton Woods agreements which he claims substantiate his argument?
I can do that.

By mutual consultation between the nations, and the like,

He is not getting me off the track; the only person getting off the track is the hon. member for Halton himself. He will never succeed; he has tried that before. Let me read once more what is said in the government white paper, which was the first official government pronouncement after Bretton Woods:
Having regard to the widespread character of our trade, the government attaches special importance .also to the reconstitution of multilateral trade on a firm basis and arrangements under which the proceeds of our exports may be spent wherever we desire to obtain our imports. '
I am reading these words so that no one will suppose I am taking the statement out of its context.
It .is with these objects in mind that the government has participated in the development of the plans for the international monetary fund and the united nations bank of reconstruction and development on which agreement among experts was reached at Bretton Woods in July last.
The monetary fund plan would assure comparative stability of exchange rates and, where change was desirable, would substitute for competitive depreciation of exchanges an orderly process of change following international consultation. It would outlaw the discriminatory currency practices which turned trade into economic warfare. I think I need read no more. Certainly the idea is definitely conveyed there that Bretton Woods would "outlaw" certain practices. look at it from a certain point of view; you must regard it in the light of all its possible results. So when we are considering a matter of this kind we are compelled to say: Now, if this measure passes will it have this result, or will it have some other result? As a member of the banking and commerce committee which studied these proposals I should like to say a few words. This committee sat in the railway room of the House of Commons, during what was zero weather outside and nearly zero inside. The committee sat about seven hours a day and really did good work trying to understand1 these proposals. But I do not think it had sufficient time to study them thoroughly and to examine enough witnesses, because we were told that this measure had to pass parliament before December 31. We called two witnesses; they were very good witnesses, but I believe we should have had more, and I am not satisfied that the committee got all the information that it should have had.
One thing which we were told in the committee and which, I think, we have to bear in mind when we are dealing with these_ proposals, is that their main object is to provide a healthier framework for better trading relations. That is a condition which we must have in this world if we are to have peace, and I hope and pray that we shall have peace for some years to come.
At the present time it looks as though Canada and other countries might have a depression, or perhaps a condition of unemployment, owing to the fact that it requires time to change over from war to peace. What is necessary is not only reconversion of industry but reconversion of our employees and readjustment of the plans that private industry has in Canada at the present time, with the throwing off of many of the controls which have been holding down industry during the war years. There is every possibility that within the next five years industry in Canada will spend at least $3,000 million of new money in expanding industries and establishing new ones, and I feel that these Bretton Woods agreements may assist in enabling Canada to dispose of the goods which these industries will produce.
After reading the final act and the bill which we have before us, I am going to be quite honest and say that I am still foggy

on some of the articles of the bill and of the final act. I am quite sure, as I said yesterday morning in the banking and commerce committee, that there are probably not more than half a dozen members of this parliament who thoroughly understand these agreements and proposals. I also said that even if they said they did, I doubted it. We had two witnesses before the committee, both expert financial men, who gave excellent evidence. They knew their stuff. Even those witnesses had to be prompted a few times; one would have to inform the other on certain things. Nevertheless they were good, and they answered any questions that were put to them, or volunteered to get the information. The member for Lethbridge asked questions; the witnesses said they would get the information and hand it in, and I imagine they looked it up in the office. I asked questions, und one of the witnesses kindly passed them on to the chairman of the committee. The chairman, I may say, did a really good job; he never squeezed us out if we wanted to get information. But these experts, financial wizards I suppose one should call them, were not quite sure of themselves on some questions. I feel that even the Minister of Finance would not know all the answers to questions we could ask him.

-there is not a man m this house who is not willing to accept it. There is not a man here who is not willing to go out and buy a ticket to help some society. He takes a chance on this, that, and the other thing, and here we have to take a chance too. Canada must take a chance on this.
It takes the rap on it.

I wish, to make a brief comment in rising to support the bill. We had an excellent explanation before the banking and commerce committee, and I think the situation is quite clear. No one tried to pretend that Bretton Woods was a magih, that it would do impossible things and solve all problems. On the other hand it was represented to us that it embodied the work of able men who had devoted much thought to the subject, and it is put forward now as the only means we have at the moment of trying to avert what might easily turn into financial chaos and the prevention of trade between countries.
The expert who gave most evidence referred to it as a breathing spell, and I was grateful to him for not having attempted to exaggerate.
What is the position? We have this agreement before us at the moment. It might have been improved, perhaps, and maybe if the experts sat down to-day they could improve it. But if we cast it aside, what do we do? We cast everything again into jeopardy, and it may be many months before another agreement can be arrived at, because ft is not easy for forty-four experts to come to an understanding. It is hard enough for forty-four ordinary men to agree on any question, and all the harder for forty-four experts.
The whole thing is summed up in my mind in an illustration that I hope will not be regarded as trivial. Certainly it will come home to a great many men who lived during the first great war. which is a little outmoded now. One almost blushes to refer to it, but it did take place. Some of you will probably remember a cartoon that appeared at that time depicting two men in a shell hole, the shells bursting all round them. They were feeling quite unhappy, and evidently had been having a strenuous argument as to what to do. The legend below the picture was: "If you knows of a better 'ole, go to it!"
I hope, as I said, this will not be regarded as a trivial illustration, but if it is, then I offer another that will certainly not be received in that light. Whatever else it may be, it certainly is not trivial. I suggest that this is an act of faith. We are living in a dangerous world where we can live only by faith. Holy ' Writ tells us that the just shall live by faith, but in these days we must all live by faith, whether we are just or unjust. Indeed, in this dangerous world, I do not know that we have much else to live by.
Someone has pointed out, very truly, I think, that in the year from June, 1940, when the other nations collapsed, to June,
