1941, when Russia came in, there was just no reason for us to -believe that we were going to win the war; yet we did believe that we would win. I say therefore that this agreement before us represents an act of faith on our part. What do I mean? I mean that it is a beginning. But if we can begin in this way, other things will follow. If we can begin by some kind of financial cooperation, it will be a help. It is only a beginning; an understanding in trade is necessary. But we can .begin with this act of faith, next summer we may have another act of faith. When trade arrangements are made they will be an act of faith for the moment too.
If the terms that have been granted to England are harsh to-day, let us work together, and have faith that they will be revised. If we can work together for a year or two years, then we can have faith that we shall strengthen our capacity to work together, and that we shall go on and on. That is why I say that it is an act of faith which I think we can all support.

I should like to sum up briefly
the position which the Social Credit group takes with respect to this whole matter before section 1 is passed. I shall not take very ipuch of the time of the committee, but I feel that I am duty bound to summarize our arguments in this way.
I listened carefully to every word that was said in this hoqse, as well as in the banking and commerce committee, with respect to Bretton Woods. I have read everything that I could get my hands on that had anything to say for or against Bretton Woods. I listened with great care to the evidence that was given in the committee by Mr. Rasminsky and Doctor Mackintosh. I have not missed one single minute of the whole of the discussions that have taken place with respect to this measure.
In the banking and commerce committee I believe I listened to the finest discussion that I have ever heard on any subject, a debate in which mind met mind in a fair and comprehensive manner. I say without any equivocation that I enjoyed that discussion immensely, and only wish with all my heart that it could be carried on with other witnesses under examination-because in the committee we had only the witnesses who were involved in the building up of the Bretton Woods agreement for the government and not any others; therefore we had no opportunity whatever to listen to the other side of the question.
As a result of all that I have been able to read and hear, I feel that the contentions of the Social Credit group have been successfully maintained; that our major criticisms of 
Bretton Woods have been proved. At no stage of the procedure from the day the resolution was introduced into the house until now have I heard anything that would in any way argue successfully against these contentions.
In the first place it is still our sincere'belief that the Bretton Woods agreement has a distinct pro-creditor-nation bias. Mr. Rasminsky's evidence showed conclusively that nowhere in the whole agreement is there any provision which will assure that creditor nations will receive imports of goods in payment for their exports to those debtor nations, which is the only way in which debtor nations may be able to avoid piling up huge burdens of interestbearing and unpayable debt. On the other hand, sir, the Bretton Woods agreement does impose upon debtor nations the responsibility of abolishing the means by which they might protect themselves against economic invasion and warfare waged by the big industrial creditor nations. Therefore in our minds the scheme stands condemned because of this fundamental weakness.
In the second place the Social Credit claim that Bretton Woods establishes a form of gold standard has been successfully substantiated-not the gold standard of 1914 or 1925; nevertheless a form of gold standard as admitted by Mr. Rasminsky in his evidence, a form of gold standard in some ways worse than any hitherto used, in that it succeeds in removing from debtor nations their means of protection against economic warfare without in any way removing the causes of that war.
In the third place there has been no satisfactory attempt to refute the Social Credit claim that article XI of the agreement provides a boycott that can and must be invoked b^ member nations against non-member nations. Therefore in this respect our claim must stand as maintained.	.
In the fourth place it was the consensus of all who spoke, and of the witnesses heard in the committee, that it would require a change of heart within each nation if Bretton Woods were ever to be made to work successfully. Our contention is, and always has been, that if a change of heart occurs amongst the nations and within the nations, there will be no need for a Bretton Woods.
It has been argued here to-day, sir, that there is no alternative, that there is no "better 'ole". In our speeches and in our arguments on a number of occasions we have put forward what is a successful and a scientific alternative to Bretton Woods, and does not contain the weaknesses or the dangers of Bretton Woods. By that I mean the London chamber of commerce proposals, the Twentieth Century Economic System. I am satisfied

Bretton Woods Agreements
that that is a better arrangement than Bretton Woods. I feel sure, Mr. Chairman, that if we had time we could prove that it is a satisfactory alternative to Bretton Woods. I am only sorry that there has been such evidence of indecent haste in trying to get this measure through, because I should like to have been able to present that alternative point by point. I understand, of course, that it would entail the necessity of convincing other nations; but, sir, that is no reason why we should not take time to examine the whole of any alternative proposal that is brought forward in the hope that we might be able to induce some of the other nations whose heart might change, as has been said, to adopt that alternative and not attach all of its faith to Bretton Woods.
My colleagues and I successfully have maintained that the whole of Bretton Woods is based upon fraudulent claims, and therefore it is not to be thought of as any mechanism for curing the world's ills.
It has been argued by some hon. members that we must live by faith. That is quite true; but I cannot look upon Bretton Woods as any act of faith. I do not like to feel that I am pinning my faith upon the same old system, the same old financial machinery that before this war brought us misery, destitution, breadlines, business stagnation, unemployment problems and all the suffering to humanity that it did. How in the name of common sense anybody can pin his faith upon that same old system under another face is beyond me. If they think, Mr. Chairman, that this will in any way change the complexion of things in the years to come, then their faith is certainly being pinned upon a shadow.
After weighing all the evidence and hearing all the arguments, my judgment is that our position has been adequately maintained, and therefore we can do no more than say we have served the interests of the people to the best of our ability. We have maintained our position right through, in spite of all efforts to hurry this up and cut us off. We have received wires and telephone calls from people all across this country asking us to continue to wage our battle, asking us to keep up the fight; they have numbered into the dozens during the course of an afternoon. But, sir, there is a limit to the endurance both of the members of this group and of this house, and I say to you that I feel we have discharged our responsibilities to the limit of our capabilities. For that reason I am going to close the case with this warning. The next few years will vindicate our judgment, and one day the Social Credit group in this house will
be credited with having done something during this phst week that might eventually save the British commonwealth of nations. I hope it will. However, in all seriousness I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that we had better look to these things which are around us; we had better examine them inside and out; we had better spare no effort in finding out exactly what we are doing. The next time any important measures like this comes up, I would suggest to the government that they get the measure into the house in plenty of time so that we may examine it thoroughly; and, having done so, make up our minds on the basis of the facts adduced and the evidence brought forward. The Social Credit members stand united in their opposition to Bretton Woods.

I rise to offer a few remarks on this measure in the hope that I may be able to create just a little doubt in the minds of my Social Credit friends as to their fears, which I think are based largely upon misunderstanding and misgivings which have no reality in fact. I do not want to weary the committee in dealing with this subject. It would take many times forty minutes to attempt to outline to the committee what the agreements contain, to say nothing of how it is hoped they will operate.
The'Bretton Woods agreements have to do with international exchange rates and1 international credits. For the moment I shall content myself with simply reading briefly the main object that is hoped to. be attained through each agreement. I refer now to article I of the agreement with respect to the international monetary fund, which states that the object this fund hopes to attain is to promote international monetary cooperation through a permanent institution which will provide the machinery for consultation and collaboration on international monetary problems. The capital involved is $8,800 million; and just here I may say that in all these figures I am about to mention the dollars are given in relation to United States funds. Canada's contribution to the fund is $300 million, of which we are to furnish twenty-five per cent in gold and the balance in Canadian currency. So that Canada's quota works out to 3-41 per cent of the fund. Then, in regard to the bank the main object, according to article I of the agreement, is:	.
To assist in the reconstruction and development of territories of members by facilitating the investment of capital for productive purposes. . .
The authorized capital is $10,000 million and Canada's contribution is $325 million, of which only two per cent is to be paid in gold
Bretton Woods Agreements

and eighteen per cent, in Canadian currency, the remainder being subject to call. In this case our total contribution, if calls were made to the full extent provided for in the act, would be 3-5 per cent of the authorized capital.
Those who oppose this measure do so on the following grounds; I may not state them in exactly the language used by individual members, but I think I can fairly sum up the objections to the Bretton Woods agreements that we have heard from the Social Credit party. Their first criticism is that Canada has not given to these agreements the time and attention which the importance of the subject demands. The next objection is that . we have acquired no substantial benefits, and that at the same time we have shackled ourselves in regard to future actions. As far as the agreements themselves are concerned their complaints are two-fold. They state the agreements will result in a return to the gold standard, and further that creditor nations are not compelled to accept payment in goods from debtor nations. I have carefully listened to all the discussion both in this house and in committee with regard to the agreements, and I believe that the objections and arguments I have just outlined are a fair resume of the position taken by the Social Credit party in opposition to these agreements. If I have erred in any way I shall thank any hon. member of that party to correct me, because I feel that if we are to get anywhere in any discussion we must at least be fair in outlining the position of our opponents.
Mr. LOW; That is fair enough.

With respect to the first criticism, that Canada has rushed into these agreements and has not taken sufficient time to consider them, I wish to say that Canada did not rush into the agreements. As far back as 1943, and prior to that, the same financial experts who performed such a wonderful job for this country in financing our war effort were studying these post-war problems; and as early as 1943 they reduced to writing suggestions they had to make in regard to the approach to this problem of international exchange and international credits. Those recommendations or suggestions were reduced to writing and submitted to the experts of other countries for consideration long before the Bretton Woods conference. Then, when the conference came, Canada sent to it a distinguished delegation, composed of the best brains in this country in regard to financial and other matters, if I may be permitted to say so.
We will not permit you to say so.

Well, I do not hesitate to say that my hon. friend would have a great deal of difficulty in choosing a stronger delegation to attend that conference. Included in the delegation was our Minister of Finance, our Minister of Justice, the governor of the Bank of Canada, the deputy minister of finance, the chairman of the foreing exchange control board, and many other competent gentlemen. These men met with the delegates of more than forty other countries at that conference; and as a result of the conference we have the Bretton Woods agreement now before the house.
In twenty-one days.

No, not twenty-one days ago. These agreements were printed in whitepaper form in 1944. They were circulated among the members of the house, and if hon. members did not read, study and ponder them, whose fault is it? Is it the fault of the government?
Not the Bretton Woods agreemenf?
Most assuredly. I hold in my hand a white paper printed by the king's printer under a date in 1944, giving the full text of the agreement, and considerable other material.

But no chance was provided
for debate.
Mr.'CLEAVER: That is a point I shall be glad to deal with. But I do say this, that so far as the government is concerned, the fullest possible information was made available to every hon. member. I received my copy months ago. I do not know when the hon. member for Lethbridge received his, but I believe he received it about the same time.

I think the hon.
member did not grasp the significance of what I said. I pointed out that these experts from forty-four nations arrived at their remarkable conclusions after twenty-one days of conference.
That is true.
A wonderful thing!

But I suggest to the hon. member that while the Bretton Woods conference lasted only from July 1 to July 22, 1944, the delegates who attended spent days, months and years in preparatory study, exchanging information back and forth, and in that way getting ready for the conference.

Bretton Woods Agreements
Bless you, you would not expect such a conference to be called without having all the spade-work and1 preparatory work done in advance.
Another hon. member has suggested that there has not been sufficient opportunity for debate in this matter, and that we did not have sufficient time in the committee on banking and commerce to discuss the measure. I should like to say a word or two in that connection.
In the committee on banking and commerce the hon. member for Lethbridge took the trouble to carry down to the committee room his copy of the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee which sat a year ago, in connection with the revision of the Bank Act. That is a revision which takes place only once in ten years, and in that instance it was long overdue. We spent day after day canvassing the advisability and wisdom of certain proposed revisions. I do not want hon. members to take offence, but I think we wasted a little time in that inquiry. I have a recollection of a few days, at least, when in my opinion we did not accomplish much.	.
I suggest to the hon. member that it is not fair to measure the time required in the banking and commerce committee for the study of, the Bretton Woods agreement with the yardstick he proposes to use. In connection with Bretton Woods we had before us an agreement negotiated by experts, after years of study, an agreement which we had no power either to amend or to vary in any way.
We had power to reject it.

Our sole task was to call before us expert witnesses so that we would, as far as it might be possible for laymen so to do, fully understand the contents of the
agreement.
It was an ultimatum.
As a result we called two men who attended the conference.
You called one.

And every member on the committee had the fullest opportunity to question those men. I did not, as chairman, shut off any of the questions, so that there was the fullest opportunity to question those men.
Only one of them.

The complaint has been made that we should have called witnesses who were opposed to the Bretton Woods agreement. I cannot understand that type of
argument. We had before us an agreement which we had either to accept or to reject. Hon. members may have noticed a press release which appears in to-day's newspapers under a Washington date, which contains the announcement that it is now apparent that just over sixty-six per cent of the subscribed membership will take place with respect to the Bretton Woods agreement by the deadline date.
That is w'hat is expected.

And included among those accepting nations is Great Britain. Is Canada to be placed in a position where we decline to support Great Britain, and where we turn down the agreement and call in experts for the purpose of securing sufficient excuse to turn them down? If Canada's 3-17 per cent is taken from the available sixty-six per cent, the necessary subscription to the agreement will not take place by the deadline date.
Does the hon. member believe that a court should hear only witnesses for the defence?
There you go! That shows the attitude of the Social Credit party. I do not want them to take offence, but I must say that if we are to acomplish anything we at least must be frank with each other.
And that is what I am doing.
Who is the defence, and who is the prosecution in connection with the Bretton Woods agreement?
But the committee heard only one side of the question.
Why does my hon. friend refer to the "defence"? It just shows the attitude.
Because the witnesses who came before the committee were defending their action.
Not at all. But it does show clearly the suspicious frame of mind under which, I am sorry to say, my hon. friends are labouring in eonnedtion with this agreement.

In the past when certain bills have been referred to committees, has it not been customary to call witnesses who might be opposed to the passage of such bills? It has been done in every committee on which I have served.

That is the purpose of the committee.

I would say this to my hon. friends, that if we had had two or three months to study this problem-
Oh, oh.
Why hadn't we?
-and if we had not been forced by the pressure of events-
Oh, oh.
-it might well be-
We met in September.

Please pehnit me to answer the question. It might well be that, even though the committee considered it unnecessary, rather than appear to act in any undemocratic fashion, my hon. friends would have been permitted1 to call witnesses, no matter how fantastic their evidence might have been.
Would you consider the evidence of Paul Einaig fantastic? That is one of the gentlemen we advocated calling.

I come now to the next objection which my friends have raised. They argue that no substantial benefits will accrue to the members from this agreement and that if Canada joins we shall be shackled in our future actions. Such words as "blockade" and other words of that kind were used.
"Blockade" was never used.

If any one expects that the millennium will come as a result of the Bretton Woods agreements, the Minister of Finance has indicated clearly that he has no such hope. I have not heard any one seriously suggest that the Bretton Woods agreements are intended to deal with more than just one segment of the post-world problem. True, it is an important part of the problem and, while world recovery cannot take place unless this part of the problem- is adequately dealt with, it is equally true that the over-all success depends upon many other factors. If the world is to become contented and prosperous there are many other matters in addition to international exchange and international credit facilities to be dealt with. Those who believe that no substantial benefits will accrue to Canada and the world as a result of the operation of the new international monetary fund and the new international bank, I consider pessimists. I suggest to my opponents that they entirely underrate the importance of international cooperation. There are some individuals in -the world who still believe that compulsion is the only way to get anything done. Happily for the world they

can be wrong. In the majority, people do not like to be coerced. The operation- of Bretton Woods is a cooperative approach as compared with dictatorship and compulsion. While the financial arrangements and facilities which are to' become available through the operation of this fund may in- the main appear to my hon. friend to be inadequate, I suggest that he and his colleagues have overlooked one feature which is quite important. Under these -agreements, we are setting up an international forumi to which nations with grievances can appeal. This conciliation board, as I would call it, will be of great advantage in further improving cooperative relations among the nations.
As to the argument that Canada is shackling herself by entering into this agreement, the agreement provides that any member can withdraw from the fund and from the bank on request.
Read article XI.

The only thing which binds members to membership in this agreement are the mutual benefits which they will get as a result of that membership. Is there anything in- that .which shackles Canada? Personally I cannot find anything. My hon. friend asked me to read -article XI. I have read article XI dozens of times to try to read into it the things which he suggests. I cannot read into article XI anything mbre than what it says. I ask hon. members to read it for themselves because it is a long article.
Explain what it means.

The operative part is this:
Each member undertakes:
(i)	not to engage in, nor to -permit any of its fiscal agencies referred to in article V, section 1, to engage in any transactions with a nonmember or with persons in -a non-member's territory which would be contrary to the provisions of this -agreement;
(ii)	not to cooperate with -a non-member . . . in practices which would be contrary -to -the provisions of this agreement . . .
The hon. member is not quoting it correctly; he left out the words "or the purposes of the fund".

If I had the time I would be glad to read the whole article. I know the hon. member has read it and I know every hon. member of the committee has this document. I will leave it at that. I do not want to hold up this measure any longer, but I should like to suggest this one feature. Under these two measures Canada is obligated to a total expenditure of 8625,000,000 to promote better cooperation internationally on exchanges and in regard to foreign credits.

Bretton Woods Agreements
When one considers the millions that we poured into winning this war, the millions we have given to UNRRA and the millions we have voted to finance export credits, would any * member dare hesitate to support a measure, the total liability under which is only $625,000,000, to further international good will and international cooperation in regard to foreign exchange and international debts?

I do not suppose that much more light can be shed on this great subject. I notice that the representatives of the parties who were represented on the banking and commerce committee have had something to say on the bill and the provisions of the agreements, and I just wanted to take a few moments of the time of the committee to indicate that I am supporting this bill as a member of the committee. I should like at least to give an idea of why I am doing that. I think the bill has some meaning, and I think the agreement has a definite meaning and has possibilities of playing a part in the future economy of the world. I hope that the prophecy of my hon. friend to my left will be absolutely untrue. I hope he can be made to believe in the possibility that he may be wrong. I consider I have as great hopes for the future of this agreement as my hon. friends have grounds for believing in its complete failure.
Perhaps I should say here that the investigations in the committee were on a very high plane. The hon. gentlemen who opposed this bill in the resolution stage and on second reading and so forth did make a contribution to the discussion and to the inquiry. The hon. member for Acadia made an outstanding contribution. Many of the questions which he raised I wanted to raise myself, and I was glad to hear the discussion which was based on them. However, I think there is an undercurrent of suspicion on the part of these hon. gentlemen which in my opinion is hardly justified. My memory of the answers of the witnesses to the questions and to' the fears which were expressed leads me to believe that those fears are groundless and that the dire effects which those hon. members anticipate as a possibility do not seem to have any basis in fact.
Someone has suggested that, in addition to being perhaps a little over-suspicious, my hon. friends to the left have not offered an alternative proposal.
We have not had the chance.

I am just going to say that. It is not clear how any group in this house could make an alternative proposal to an international agreement. That is one of the 47696-221
factors of this whole discussion which >we ought to keep in view. This is an international agreement which, as the chairman of tire banking and commerce committee has just explained, was carefully gone into and prepared for long in advance. It cannot be amended here, we cannot propose an alternative to it here. The only way we could have an alternative to an agreement of this kind is to go out and make another international agreement, which would take quite some time, and we do not have enough time to do that, so that is quite impossible. However, since that is so, and since we cannot amend the terms of the agreement or, at this session, create an alternative, I think it is only fair that those who oppose the agreement as it is should be able to set forth the general principles upon which it might be possible to arrive at a better agreement. I believe my hon. friends think they have done that. Some of us disagree; but I do not want to argue that point here; we shall have to differ on that point, for the moment at least, without taking time to go into the details of the difference.
I think, however, my hon. friends on the left should agree on this point. They have pointed out, more often and perhaps more effectively than most of us, the influence of international finance on international policy. If we are to prevent the evil influences of international finance, and if we are to obtain democratic control of the instruments of finance international, surely we must follow the projects of international finance into the international field. There is no possibility of preventing an international undertaking by any kind of national action, and if you are to have democratic control of international finance it can be had only by the creation of an international body to do the controlling. This agreement, with all the faults it may have-and I am' quite prepared to say that from my point of view it has some faults- is, in my opinion, an outstanding agreement in this particular, that an international organization is about to make an experiment, and a very important one, in international financing. Provision is made in this agreement whereby at least some financing can be done without one having to go cap in hand to the international bankers. Although the finances which have been provided in this agreement may properly be regarded by hon. members as inadequate for what it may be called upon to do, and this may very well prove to be true, it is a beginning, and to the extent that it is the beginning of an international organization which provides funds for the use of

Bretton Woods Agreements
Or gives it away.

Or gives it away, yes. I
think that phase of the agreement should be an excellent lesson in international economies; and I would say that in the practice of this, nations that have large surpluses to export and are tardy about permitting exchange of goods for their surpluses, will learn a great lesson.	.

May I say just a word or two in summing up some of the advantages, and then I shall have finished.
In the first place, I have emphasized the importance of the international effort. It is an international organization tackling a problem which is international in character and which no individual government could possibly solve. Second, one of its tasks is to stabilize exchange rates, and to make available for that purpose a fund which will be accessible to the nations that happen to get into difficulty; and this, without having to be at the mercy of international bankers.
Another feature of the bill or of the agreement is, of course, the international bank. That too, with its ten billions of capital, wiii be an important factor in the future economy of the world, and has great possibilities of extension. There are vast territories in the world which are backward and undeveloped; and if we are to increase our standard of living here and throughout the world, then those backward countries must be helped to develop their resources, so that they too, can raise their standards of living in order to consume more of our goods in exchange for those which they have to send to us. If private enterprise does not want to go into these countries alone for fear of losing something, we have [DOT] an international fund which will be guaranteed by the country that does the borrowing which makes it possible to furnish investment capital in backward parts of the world, which may well play an important part in the postponing at least of the worst phases of a depression which may be upon us at any time.
The claim that this is the gold basis is both true and untrue-I was going to say false, and I do not know whether untrue is the same thing. What I mean is this. The witness, Mr. Rasminsky, said that it was a phase of the gold standard; that is to say, that the gold standard is used merely as a measuring stick, and it is just as good a measuring stick, he argues, as an index figure. I do not know whether that is true or not. I would rather . have an index figure myself. I am not very much interested in gold measuring sticks. But it is used only as a means of making up trade balances between nations and the feature of the gold standard which most of us object to most strenuously means that you can, because of the g'old standard, limit the currency and credit of your nation to such an extent as to practically starve your people in the midst of abundance. That has been very largely true in some instances. That feature of it is not

Bretton Woods Agreements
in practice in this international agreement, so that it is really not true to say that we have the gold standard which figured in our contentions years ago.
The next point is that the agreement does not mean that Canada or any other country which ratifies the agreement must go on the gold basis. Canada is not on the gold basis, thank heaven, and I do not suppose it wants to be; and if it ever tries to be on that basis I for one will do my best to keep it off.
Here is the last point. If creditor nations do not accept goods in payment for their exports; if under this agreement they do not wish to do so, we shall be no worse off than we are now, not the slightest bit in the world. That is what they do now and what they have always done. On the other hand, the whole object of the agreement is to encourage those nations which adopt it to do just that; that is to say, to accept goods in exchange for their favourable balances.
May I call the attention of the committee to the proposal made between the United States government and the government of the United Kingdom for the expansion of world trade and employment. Here we have what might be said to be a necessary corollary of the agreement we are discussing, that if these trade agreements are not effected after this agreement, then of course it will prevent the Bretton Woods agreement from accomplishing its purpose.
I believe there are great possibilities in this agreement. If it fails, as my hon. friend thinks it will, I shall not be surprised but I shall be greatly disappointed. I am hoping that this undertaking, which we have started with such little enthusiasm, which seems to have no friends anywhere, may turn out to be the beginning of that world government which I believe is essential if we are to save the human race.

I wish to say^ with regard to this matter generally that we in the C.C.F. party have protested yearly against living conditions among the Indians, the want that has existed there, and in many cases the attitude of the government. We have protested also against injustices committed by the Indian affairs. branch, in that many of the treaties signed with these people have apparently been broken. It is encouraging. then, to find that since the present minister has taken over the affairs of this department there has been a change in attitude, and that some of the reforms and changes we advocated in the past are apparently in process of being attended to.
One cam scarcely be charged with speaking politically when he refers to Indian affairs, when it is remembered that the Indians have no vote. In my view one of the chief defects

in the department has been that the Indians have had no way in which their voice could be heard by the federal authorities.
We note with a good deal of pleasure the fact that the government is apparently undertaking some revision of the Indian Act. Although thus far no action has been taken to place amendments before the house, I would expect that before his estimates are completed the minister would give us some information on the point and at that time possibly he would tell us when those changes might be expected to take the form of legislation.	'
Within the past year the Indians of Canada have undertaken to organize themselves in each of the provinces. They have gathered together in convention, and have been successful in sending delegates from all parts of Canada. Last September one of those conventions was held in Ottawa, at which time there were presented to the government briefs in which were set out certain complaints they had in connection, with the administration of Indian affairs.
One of the suggestions had to do with a proposed amendment to the Indian Act, so as to give Indians some voice in the administration of their affairs. The Indian considers that he is treated too much as a child, and in my view the time has come when we should look upon the Indian population as humans, with rights to citizenship. They need not be treated entirely as wards. The policy under the Indian Act has been to keep them subdued to such an extent that their capacity and ability have been smothered. Surely this is not good.
New Zealand is one of "the countries which in this connection has taken a forward step. The Maoris have been granted rights of citizenship to the extent that they now have representation in that part of the New Zealand system of government which would correspond to our House of Commons. Their representatives sit in that legislative body, and act in connection with the administration of Maori affairs.
Surely the time has come when a similar step should be taken in Canada so that an opportunity would be given to those thousands of Indians within our boundaries who might wish to have representation in the affairs of the country, and more particularly some voice in the administration of their own affairs.
I believe the minister will agree that the Indian organizations in Canada have shown that they have capacity and ability. Their attitude has been one of willingness and they have shown an anxiety to cooperate. I believe any assistance the government could give to

Supply-Indian Affairs
help them organize would be appreciated, because they operate with only limited means. It is my understanding that the minister has seen fit to* assist them to the extent of providing travelling expenses to their conventions. That is a new procedure, and one which is much appreciated by the Indian population.
I believe they have written several letters to the minister expressing their appreciation of his attitude.
I suggest that in the revision of the act the government should consider the fact that until the Indians of Canada have representation in the Indian affairs branch, to which they must appeal for the settlement of their grievances, they will feel that they have not had proper representation, or proper opportunity for the redress of their grievances.
I note that this year there is an increase of about $1 million in expenditures for the health and welfare of Indians across Canada. This increase, which represents about sixteen per cent of the total, is all to the good, and is a step toward wiping out some of the prevailing wrongs. Conditions among many of the Indians are deplorable; I have never seen suffering such as I have seen in some of the Indian reserves.
The Indians have expressed a desire to have an over-all inquiry into their conditions across Canada, so that a study may be made of those conditions from which evils arise, with a view to effecting remedies. I believe the department has not seen its way clear to grant the request for an inquiry, but is considering changes in the act, without such an inquiry having been made. An inquiry of the kind suggested could do much good.
Within the past two weeks the executive of the North American Indian brotherhood met in Ottawa and, in the absence of an inquiry, they have made suggestions to the government respecting revisions to certain sections in the Indian Act. They direct attention first to section 18, which deals with the entitlement of a band to receive benefits. There is the feeling that their own Indian councils have the capacity to decide who should and who should not come within the band. Section 18 now reads.
The superintendent general (minister) may, from time to time, upon the report of an officer, or other person specially appointed by him to make an iifquiry, determine -who is or who is not a member of any band of Indians entitled to share in the property and annuities of the band.
2. The decision of the superintendent general (minister) in any such matter shall be final and conclusive, subject to an appeal to the governor in council.
Then section 40 states:
No person shall buy or otherwise acquire from any band or irregular band of Indians or from any Indian and no Indian shall sell or otherwise dispose of to any one other than a member of the band, any cattle or other animals of any kind from any reserve in the province of Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta or the Territories without the written consent of the Indian agent.
The band still feels that the Indian agent in this respect has been granted too much power.
I believe that some years ago this section had merit, but to-day the Indians are in a position to give proper judgment as to who should sell cattle and materials off the reserves. In the early days there were occasions when drovers and other unscrupulous persons-used to come to the reserves and practically steal cattle from the Indians. At that time this section was a proper safeguard. However, to-day I believe that the band should make decisions of this kind, and that under the present system the Indian should be given a full report of the sale price of his cattle, to whom they were sold and the date upon which they were sold.
Then, section 52 has to do with the power of the governor in council to remove any Indian band from the place in which it is at present situated. This gives absolute power to the minister, or the officials at his department, to move a band, if in the opinion of th-ose officials the band is situated too close to a town or city. The Indian band has no say in the matter at all.
Section 93 contains particular powers. It reads:
The governor in council may, with the consent of a band, authorize and direct the expenditure of any capital moneys standing at the credit of such band in the purchase of land as a reserve for the band or as an addition to its reserve, or the possessory rights of a member of the band in respect of any particular parcel of land on the reserve, or in the purchase of cattle, implements or machinery for the band, or in the construction of permanent' improvements upon the reserve of the band, or such works thereon or in connection therewith as, in his opinion, will be of permanent value to the band, or will, when completed, properly represent capital, or in the making of loans to members of the band to promote progress, no such loan, however, to exceed in amount one-half of the appraised value of the interest of the borrower in the lands held by him.	.
In the event of a band refusing a consent to the expenditure of such capital moneys as the superintendent general (minister) may consider advisable for any of the purposes mentioned an subsection one of this section, and it appearing to -the superintendent general (minister) that such refusal is detrimental to the progress or welfare of the bahd, the governor in council may, without the consent of the band, authorize and direct the expenditure of such capital for such of the said purposes as may be considered reasonable and proper.

Recently there was passed by this house under the minister's guidance a bill taking away from an Indian reserve, I think it was the Stony Indian band in Alberta, certain water power rights. The minister stated that the arrangements with regard to that sale were carried on Without the consent of the band. In view of the rights of these Indians, in view of the fact that this is their property, I think the band should have been consulted about the matter so that they, would know what was being done. Section 99A gives considerable power to the agent. It reads:
At meetings of the council the agent for the reserve, or his deputy appointed for the purpose with the consent of the superintendent general ([DOT]minister), shall
(a)	preside, and record the proceedings;
(b)	control and regulate all matters of procedure and form, and adjourn the meeting to a time named or sine die.
Is it not time that the Indian band themselves were permitted to carry on their own business at these band meetings? They could go to the agent for advice instead of being constantly placed under the control of these persons.
Section 102 deals with taxation. The Indian considers that he is not getting the rights and privileges of his white brothers. Since he does not share in the benefits of taxation, he feels that there are certain taxes to which he should not be subject. The Indians have shown a willingness to cooperate with the government and I believe that if there were proper discussion between the officials of the department and the representatives of the North American Indian brotherhood executive an understanding could be reached.
I do not think they object to paying taxes on income earned off the reserve; but in some cases, Quebec for example, these Indians have homes on the reserve. Some of them have electricity in their houses and they must pay a special tax on . that. They feel that being on a reserve they should not have to pay that. They consider that a single person should not be taxed on income less than SI,000 a year and that if married, he should be exempt up to $2,000. There are matters like this which require the consideration of the department and which should be modified.
The Indians have shown a tremendous willingness to cooperate. They appreciate what the minister has done, and they are willing to go all the way with him in an effort to have what they consider wrongs redressed. If the government will do these things I am sure it will have the support of all hon. members. A few weeks ago we had a discussion on, a resolution which would have

given the Indians the right to old age pensions. Hon. members on all sides and of every party supported that. Unfortunately some hon. members talked so lo^g, whether deliberately or not I do not know, and it was impossible to have a vote. Surely the expressions of opinion given in this house are sufficient to let the minister know just how the representatives of the people of Canada feel in regard to this matter. If there is any possibility at all of carrying out the suggestions that have been made and giving these people who were first in our midst, the real Canadians, an opportunity to make a contribution to the Dominion of Canada, it should be done. We are voting millions for the welfare of the Indians, but let us give them an opportunity and they will take care of themselves. These people can take care of themselves; they can fend for themselves if given an opportunity.
The educational system for the Indian is wrong is several particulars. According to the latest report of the department, the number of Indians in Canada between the ages of seven and sixteen years is 26,000. The average attendance of Indians in schools, residential and day and others, is 13,257. Only one-half of the Indian children in Canada are receiving training. I realize that there is something to be said about the difficulties encountered in the far north with these people moving about, but the matter of education should receive special consideration in view of the fact that these people are not yet living under the same standards as the white people.
Go to some of these schools and you will find them teaching Indian girls how to cook on an electric plate or how to run an electric washing machine. When they go back to the reserve they are just discontented. These people have capacities as fishermen, as hunters and as woodsmen. I wish to compliment the department upon what they have done in the way of fur farming. These people have a great capacity to work and provide for themselves and they could make a contribution to our country. Early in life we should discover what capacities they have and then train them along those lines. If we do that we shall soon have doctors, nurses and missionaries who. will go out among these people and help to lift them up. If the government will continue with this policy I am sure it will have the support of every phrty in this house. I have offered these few suggestions in the hope that the government will do something along these lines. I can assure the minister that he will receive the cooperation, of every one here.

I am not going to be long, because of the late stage of the session at which these estimates have come before the committee, and also because we know we must get them through promptly since the minister has an important engagement in the far west which it is imperative that he keep. But I wish to make one or two suggestions, particularly because he is a new minister in an old department.. I am sure that all hon. members who have any experience as regards Indian affairs want to help him in his great task. I personally have strong hopes that he will do a fine job when he gets thoroughly accustomed to the work of the department.
First, I suggest that in his own good time he consider setting up a parliamentary committee, a special committee or otherwise, consisting of members of this house and of the senate, to inquire thoroughly into the whole problem of Indian affairs. It is quite a long time since this was last done, and I feel sure that everyone will admit that the time has come, owing to the real advance which the Indians have made, when new regulations could be prepared which would have much more beneficial consequences to them and to the country generally.	.
I further suggest to the minister that he urge on the government, contrary to the practice, to have his departmental estimates brought in early. During the sixteen years I have been here they have been introduced almost at the very last living hour of the session. My good friend the hon. member for Vancouver Centre puts estimates through rapidly. I am not finding any fault about that, but I recall that at the time he sat on this side of the house the estimates did not go through so fast. However, I give him credit for getting departmental estimates through; I am sure he would have made a good business manager.
In the discussion which would probably arise in such a committee as I have suggested, the matter of having Indian representatives in the house might well have a place. As the minister probably knows, the natives of South Africa, the Kaffir peoples, have either four or five representatives in the South African parliament. So, too, in New Zealand, the original native race is represented' in the legislature as referred to by a previous hon. member. The native races of these dominions are no better than our own, and I am of opinion that the proposal would be well worth considering, although I have no definite suggestions as to how this should be put into effect. In South
Africa the Kaffirs select their representatives in the house; whether they are represented by Kaffirs or whites I am unable to say at the moment, but in any event they are there, watching the interests of the millions of Kaffirs who live in South Africa. The problem of Indian representation is, I am sure, worth considering.
I myself 'have visited1 many reservations, perhaps twenty-five, and some in remote areas. I question whether any hon. member other than my leader has visitedi the two reservations on the Saskatchewan river, Chemahawin and Moose Lake. Probably he has visited both of them; they are remote and seldom visited by the white man. On lake Nipigon are three reserves. My suggestion to the minister is: when you visit them, go alone if you can, or take your secretary with you; you do not need anyone to tell you about this or that; when you get in a reservation there will be plenty of people to tell you all about it, and your conclusions will be your own, not what the agent or some other official tells you. I have made many surveys and I have seen a lot of reserves, but I am not going to take time to talk about them to-night.
A number of the reserves have fairs. One is the reservation of western Ontario, of the Delaware tribe, of which I am proud to be an honorary chief. They call themselves the grandfathers of Indian tribes. As the minister knows, their name is derived from Lord De la Warre, who settled on the Delaware river. They have a fair every year. A day or two ago I had a letter from their chief, Fred Stonefish, suggesting that I put up some prizes-which I am going to do-for the best-dressed folks in Indian regalia at the fair. I believe the time'has come to encourage them to take pride in their past. If you do that they will have more pride in the country to which they now belong. There should also be an effort to encourage them to exhibit at their fairs those things they make which are the distinctive product of their culture, and steps should be taken to help them to dispose of these products.
When the minister again goes to northern Manitoba I suggest that he visit Moose lake. If he will notify Thomas Lamb, Mr. Lamb will bring his diesel engined boat to The Pas and take him down river. I urge him to go down the Saskatchewan river and have a chat with Mr. Lamb about fur production. He is the real father of the development of the fur business in the Saskatchewan delta. He spent his own money bringing in pumps from the United States and pumping the water into the dried-out marshes. I know that the government of Manitoba-and this government also
Supply-Indian Affairs

-is now assisting in the production of furs in the Saskatchewan delta. But let the minister talk to the man who knows. I know Mr. Lamb intimately; he is the father of that business. I suggest to the minister, consult with him and talk to the officials after that, and you will get a new slant on the whole fur-production business.
A word or two more. The Indian educational system can be vastly improved. One day some estimates came in here relating to three reserves on lake Nipigon; and after what came out here I determined to go and see for myself. I engaged a diesel engine boat and went down the river from Willett. I visited the three reservations in that district, and I am bound to say that one of the schools was rather backward. I will not say which one, but there I saw a young girl teaching, a very nice and comely girl, but without the qualifications of a teacher. I found no child beyond the part second book in a school of twenty-eight. I will not elaborate on the question of Indian education except to say that in the Indian school on the Moravian reservation in Kent county the children have attained a high standard for a common school. The Indian schools are not all backward by any means, but some are not what they should be.
I am going to close with this comment. In Kent county on the reservation of the Moravian band of Indians it is proposed to have an international commemoration service in 1950 to which a good many eminent persons will be invited. The minister knows, or if he does not know personally he will have read in the history of western Ontario and particularly of Kent county, that the Delaware tribe came there in 1792, one of the largest branches of the whole Delaware Indian tribe in America to-day. They came with a. missionary, the Reverend David Zeisberger, who was accompanied by a famous assistant Sense-man. It is proposed to make 1950 an important year not only in the history of the Indians themselves but as commemorating the 137th anniversary of the death of the last and greatest of the Indian chiefs of those days, Tecumseh, who did so much to preserve Ontario as part of the British domain. To that international commemoration service we hope to invite the President of the United States, because one of his predecessors, General Harrison, was in command of the American army at the battle of the Thames, later becoming President of the United States. Several of the governors of states also commanded forces at that battle. We hope to have present at the commemoration the governors of Michigan, Kentucky, Ohio, Penn-

sylvania, states all represented at the Battle of the Thames. Later on, I will take the matter up with the minister.

I will not detain the committee, but I simply want to concur in what my colleague said. I will not repeat it, but I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I am more hopeful of the Indian situation than I was a year ago and I wish to congratulate the minister. It may seem strange to congratulate ministers, hon. gentlemen sitting onj that side-

I am reluctant to do so, but where praise is deserved I will not withhold it. I wish to congratulate also Mr. Hoey and Mr. Allan of the department, with whom I have been constantly in touch. On this occasion I have no grievances to bring before the committee, having already discussed matters with the department. I must say that they gave me wonderful cooperation.
There is one matter that my colleague omitted to bring before the minister. The residential schools are not up to the number they should be this year, for the reason, that it pays the Indian better to keep his children at home and get the family allowance instead of sending them to school. That is a problem which will have to be solved in the near future. We may find it necessary to turn the residential schools into vocational schools, building little schools, and let the children stay at home.
I hope that in his negotiations with the provincial governments the minister will see to it that the Indians are protected. I would draw his attention to the situation in St. Peter's reserve. If the land is handed over to the provincial government it will be necessary to protect the rights of the Indians as lar as their hay claim is concerned. The Indians with whom I come in contact on the reserve in my constituency insist upon the appointment of a royal commission, but perhaps if the department continues to move at the rate it is going now we may not need 'that royal commission. The extra money that has been voted for hospitals and the care of the sick is a step in the right direction. I would ask the minister to make some provision for the Indians at Norway House in the way of a muskrat conservation scheme. I have talked the matter over with his officials and I hope it will be given serious consideration,

I should like to say a few words on this vote in view of the remarks made by hon. members. It is gratifying indeed to note the tone of the discussion on the

Supply-Indian Affairs
Indian estimates, and it was also gratifying to me to find expressions of opinion of the type we heard when we were discussing old age pensions for Indians.
I think it can be said with a good deal of truth that at no time in many years have the affairs of Indians been so focused in the minds of the people of this country as they are to-day. I believe that members are expressing views which are being expressed throughout the whole country, that the affairs of the Indians must be attended to in a manner in which they have not hitherto been considered, and the aspirations and hopes of the Indians must be to some extent fulfilled.
I have had the pleasure of meeting the brotherhood of which the hon. member for Yorkton spoke, first in September when I addressed them and then again this week. They have made many proposals to which the hon. member himself has referred and of which I have a note. It was impressed upon me that they represent a particular part of the country and that that part of the country had its own particular problems, which they, were expressing.
It may be that we shall find after investigation that these problems affecting individual bands are not general throughout the country, but I am convinced that, in order that Indian affairs should be properly conducted and, as it were, a charter prepared for Indians, something further will have to be done. I did indicate, when speaking in the debate on old age pensions, that we had under consideration a policy for dealing with Indian affairs, and I mentioned then the question of a royal commission. Ever since then I have regretted having referred to the subject, because I have had so many representations as to persons who might wish to act on the commission.
A suggestion was made by the hon. member for Davenport with regard to a special committee of the house to be constituted along with members of the senate. The suggestion is that we might be able to arrive at a conclusion whereby we could deal as far as possible with the problems of the Indians. I am satisfied that unless we get some united representation of the Indians throughout the country we shall not be very successful. I believe that the isolated expressions of opinion coming from the bands or groups of individual Indians will not meet the situation, and I have made the suggestion to those with whom I have been discussing the matter -this band of Indians and the brotherhood- that there should be provincial organization. In fact, I believe it was first indicated by one 47696-222
of the members of the delegation that, in his view, the only way in which these matters could be focused and brought forward in a more representative and concrete form would be by means of provincial organizations throughout the dominion.
In the course of the discussion it was illustrated that throughout Canada many organizations have started in the provincial field and could broaden out into the federal field. If it could be broadcast among the Indians that if they were to form, within each of the provinces, their own organizations composed of officers and men of integrityin whom they have confidence, in the evolution of time they may arrive at that date which the hon. member for Davenport spoke about when he said there might be Indians 'on the floor of this house representing that body of people in the Dominion of Canada. I am satisfied that we must have an expression of opinion from the Indians throughout the whole of the Indian population. It seems to me the best way in which it can be done, although I may change my mind after due consideration, is to have a special committee set up to which the Indians can make representation. I am satisfied that a body of men such as we have here, and a committee such as could be formed from members of this house who are deeply interested in the affairs of the Indians, would be able to arrive at an act which would largely embody the desires of the Indians.
I do not fail to recognize the great magnitude of the undertaking. Along with that charter for the Indians, as one may call it, there must also be intelligent administration. Upon the administration of an act depends its success. For that reason I am hopeful that at the next session of parliament we shall be able to introduce a draft bill, the details of which shall be subject to discussion, and to which I shall invite the best attention and consideration of the wisdom of the members of this house.

To complete the story in Manitoba, I am glad to be able to inform the Committee that an agreement was entered into with the provincial government to establish in the northern part of that province fourteen fur administrative units which take in practically all the northern part of Manitoba. In Saskatchewan a board known as the northern Saskatchewan conservation board was created in 1939 and an agreement was entered into with the provincial government for the carrying out of a cooperative arrangement to restore the fur industry as a principal means of livelihood to the Indian and half-breed population. A number of small projects were carried out by the board and as well many other investigations were made. I am sure the members of the committee will have been interested in the progress that has been made in our programme. Muskrat farming and the development of areas for beaver on a large scale is an industry of tremendous possibilities. There are millions of acres susceptible to this form of development. Our experience of public development of rat and beaver projects in Canada has been along a road leading to the goal of material assistance and a better way of life to the humbler crosssection of our Canadian social order. In speaking to the question of immigration, I realize that the only immigration the Canadian people are interested in at the present time is the return of the service men and women from overseas as quickly as possible. When they are back in suitable jobs, again leading normal lives, this country can turn its attention to immigration. That seems a little closer at hand than would first appear, from the statement made, I think yesterday, by the Minister of National Defence, who gave us some information as to how quickly they are coming home. I am sorry he is not in his seat at the moment, because I want not only to thank him for what he was doing, but to let him know that a great number of people in this country, particularly the young women and the mothers, are not only glad that he is bringing the boys back home alive, but that he is bringing them home alone, too.
My particular purpose in rising-and I believe this is an important question-is to bring to the attention of-the committee the needs of the country' with respect to immigration, so that the question can be not only surveyed but studied, and assessments made in the light of our attributes, facilities and possibilities. I say that not only because this is a country of security, but because it is one of opportunity. We have now the time to plan what we are going to do to-morrow. We have perhaps six months, or possibly a little longer than that, so that we can carefully and ambitiously make our plans.
Those plans have to follow a view different from that formerly held in this country, because in former years the great source of immigrants has been the British isles. But anyone who knows anything about the British isles-and I.could quote authorities to support me in this-knows that they will be able to absorb all their own man-power for the next five or ten years, and that they will have to keep everybody in Great Britain. We know, too, that Great Britain is suffering from a declining birthrate.
It is true that some of the Royal Air Force personnel who trained in this country will be anxious to return here, and that they will be welcomed. Some of them may be permitted to come to this country. But the great well which we formerly had in the British isles will be dried un for many years to come.
When we turn to the Scandinavian countries, none of us would for a moment suggest that Finland, Norway, or Sweden would be a source of immigrants for some considerable time in the future.
Turning once again to continental Europe, we must realize that, too, is of a doubtful nature, because Europe to-day is going through not only a sortipg but also a settling process. They need all available man-power in Europe, first to keep what to some minds for the present seems to be a doubtful peace, and, second, to rebuild destroyed Europe. Many hon. members who were over there will know that when I say "destroyed" I mean just exactly that. That is going to be a longtime and a full-time job, we can depend upon it. [DOT]
There has come about recently in this country a new realization, a new perspective and a new understanding on the question of immigation, and it has come from some rather unexpected placed. I hold in my hand a report of the Imperial Bank of Canada, whose president, Mr. R. S. Waldie, says:
It should be noted that the reduction of the general overhead expenses of our economy depend in large measure on an increase in the density of our population which lessens especially the transportation and administration charges per unit of production.
Them, Mr. McGowan, director of the Canadian National Railways, said on November 30:
The admission of more people would increase Canada's prosperity and _ assist in its development. When the dominion's population is doubled, it will raise the standards of living.
I quote again from the Toronto Globe and Mail of December 5, in which Mr. J. S. Duncan, president of the Massey-Harris Company Limited, is reported to have said in a Montreal speech:
Canada has to be realistic about the future economic position of the country and the necessity of expanding export trade as well as the home market for Canadian goods. _ He recommended adoption of a selective immigration policy to increase the population.
The general tenor of these press comments from different sources is that there is a need for more people in this country, and the approach is such that plans must be realistic, intelligent, and rational. From the economic point of view it will be said that we need purchasing power, and we need those with

whom we may divide the national debt- unless someone will devise some method of getting rid of it otherwise.
I do not want to proceed further without expressing a word of thanks to the government of Canada which, in the midst of the war, offered not only sanctuary but a haven and hospitality to great numbers of people who were refugees, who came to this country from all nations, and who helped in our war effort. The government realized that, and in due time gave them permanent landing in Canada. In view of those landings, and' in view of the services they have rendered the country, in due time they have earned the right to be joined by whatever remnants there may be of their families still remaining in continental Europe; and I hope the minister will put this high on his priority list.
Last week in the committee on veterans affairs some startling figures were revealed, and I believe they will prove of interest to hon. members. We have about 17,000 returned men training for various jobs, but of that number only 1,600 are training for the building trades. At the time these figures were revealed, I said that I thought it was a tragedy to find that we have not a larger number who are joining what might be described as the aristocrats of labour. Canadians are not soft; we proved that in this war, and even before the war. Our standard of living is fairly high, and we are striving to improve it.
Hon. members may interpret these figures as they wish, but it strikes me that we have about reached the stage in this country where we need some hired help on our farms. We need some others who will do the heavy work. In my short experience in public life I have had something to ,do with unemployment, andi I know something of the hardships unemployed people have suffered. But in all my experience the people who, somehow, were always able to make a living were the carpenters, the bricklayers and the plumbers. We have always looked upon those trades as offering honourable and fine ways of earning a living. I think there is something sad when one considers the fact that young men are not entering these trades which offer good prospects in the immediate future, particularly for the next ten years.
My suggestion is that the government have both a short-term and a long-term policy. I would say that its short-term policy should be based fifst upon humanitarian principles. All that many citizens in this country have left is to be found somewhere in continental Europe, and I suggest that they should be given the first opportunity to come to this country. Next, not only must we open our

doors, but we must open our hearts to the orphans of Europe-and there are thousands of them over there-who in the future will pay such great dividends. I do not know whether we have made any commitments during the war, but if we have we would in due course honour them.
Then, I think we should have a long-term policy. We must be able to assess our future needs, and our ability to absorb, because the post-war immigration problem will be a very heavy one. I think all hon. members agree with me when I say that we need people, and that we have to do something about it.
My suggestion to the minister is that he divorce immigration from agriculture and set up as quickly as possible after we come back next year an immigration committee to make a special study of this particular problem, to hear evidence, to make a survey and then to make recommendations. For instance, for a long time and up until quite recently labour has had a fear of immigration. I do not think they are of that view now, but they have held that view for too long. I think industry should be heard, and business, the church, veterans, economists, scientists, professional men and anyone who can contribute to the cause, so that the committee could form a broad plan for the general welfare of Canada. The committee could study the question of assimilation, so that we can bring in people who believe in our way of life. It could give consideration to the part that people had played in this war, to their physical attributes, to their character, skills, training, trades, commercial experience, business attributes and agricultural experience.
If we set up this committee we could have a plan ready long before the beginning of the following year. Not only could we have men in the field; we could be ready to take in whoever we could absorb. In the past our policy has been based on pressure by special groups. That method is now outmoded and outworn; the time for that has long passed. It does not fit into the present world. All our thoughts and all our legislation in the past were pointed toward exclusion and restriction;
I think we have come to the time when we have not only to admit but to welcome people to our country. I am not suggesting an open door; I am not suggesting a closed door; I think the time has come for the door to be left ajar.
While I am on my feet I cannot help saying to the minister that we have on our statute books at the present time a great deal of racial nonsense. It is time to get it off the books. Racism is bad whether it comes from

Supply-Immigration
Canadians or Germans. The exponents of racism are now attending the Nuernberg rally and they do not like it. We are glad they do not like it. It is not our business to emulate them in any way at all.
We must plan our immigration policy of the future and we must not be afraid of planning. There is nothing wrong about democratic planning. We have to assess our needs and know our ability to absorb. We should budget for people the same way as we budget for everything else. We have reached that stage. Men- and women in this country plan their families and sometimes they make mistakes. We may make mistakes too, but it is time that we started to plan our Canadian family.
Sometimes I wonder, with the world fighting for liebestraum, if we have a moral right to sit on half a continent which has the largest amount of arable land in all the continent and close the door to the rest of the peoples. I submit that we have arrived at a time when we can formulate a policy that will stand up. We can no longer afford to deal with immigration on the basis of expediency and prejudice. Our economy is undergoing a serious change and we have to change with it. We are no longer a frontier land; we are on the top of the heap of the middle powers. We have obligations and responsibilities and we must live up to them.
I suggest to the minister that he lose no time after we come back to set up an immigration committee to study and plan so that we can do something intelligent about it. I am not going to say anything about his department for the last four, five or six years. Let us agree that it was dormant; there was a war on, but there is no excuse for not doing anything now, because we have time on our hands. It will be April or May before we have everybody back in this country, although I hope it will be sooner. We should lay our plans and get our policy ready. We should have our agents where they are needed and be ready to take people into this country; we should have all the necessary machinery ready.
I said a few moments ago that the people of Europe will not be available. Do not be mistaken; the people of Europe want to come here but their governments will not permit them because they need them at home. The Minister of Fisheries will remember when we had to put up signs in Europe in Dutch or French, meaning immigration impossible. Otherwise those people kept bothering us. They were all anxious to leave the country, but the governments need them at home. I
know very well that the Dutch government has its plans for its colonies, and so has the Belgian government. They have neglected their colonies for too long and so they have trouble on their hands. If there are to be people to export, they will send them out there. It seemed to be the desire of every boy I met to leave those countries. It will not be just as easy as it seems. We must be careful and make sure to have our plans ready. If we plan well we can make much of it.

As I understand it, the present policy is that if a Norwegian is

temporarily in Canada and has married a Canadian girl he is entitled to remain. The eases of the single men are judged on their individual merits. I believe that is correct; is that not. so?
Yes.
