It is quite obvious that the committee will not have much time to discuss Canada's immigration policy at any length in the remaining two days of this session.
One day.

But this extremely important and urgent problem should receive proper consideration at the earliest opportunity during the next session. I should like to make one or two general references on the subject before dealing briefly with a specific aspect of immigration.
First, let me read one or two passages and observations of the Edmonton chamber of commerce report dated October 15, 1945, which indicates their stand on the subject of immigration, and with a good number of whose recommendations I agree. The report states:
Your committee is definitely in favour of a national immigration policy designed to increase the population of Canada ... It believes that an increase in population through immigration would improve Canada's position and influence in world affairs and would strengthen also the power of the British commonwealth of nations. It would enable this country particularly to adjust her domestic economy by providing more diversified and larger home markets, and it would also reduce the per capita expenses of the many government and other services which a modern nation is expected to provide for her citizens.
Canada has tremendous assets in its resources of raw materials, in the strong foundation which - has been established for an elaborate system of transportation, in its productive and industrial equipment, which has become increasingly strengthened during the war, and in the quality of its present population. This country has maintained its democratic institutions and has shown that it believes in a policy of voluntary cooperation, having regard and respect for a policy that individual freedom and personal initiative should be retained within the framework of a scheme of collective action and security.

I should like to mention one or two other points raised in this report. I believe that they are presented, in a most vivid and clear manner:
That machinery should be set up immediately with a view to the formation of a policy designed to attract to Canada those elements in the population of Europe, and possibly of certain .other countries who would best contribute to the economic stability and cultural growth of this dominion without imperilling the free institutions . . .
I agree wholeheartedly with the remark made to-night by the hon. member for Spadina that we should undertake to study this problem closely and carefully at the next session, and I believe that the question should be referred to a committee of this house and properly investigated and studied so that we may arrive at logical conclusions.
I find that the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of November 10, 1945, in discussing editorially the order in council of October 26, 1945, granting official admission to refugees who entered Canada during the war-and at this time I should like to compliment the minister and the government upon passing that order in council; I think it w'as the only stand they could properly take and I am glad they did take it-points out:
In these circumstances the Canadian government has taken the wise course of permitting these people to remain indefinitely in Canada. No doubt arrangements will be made whereby those who desire to do so may acquire Canadian citizenship and proceed to build new lives in this country . . . But the point of the new regulation permitting these people to stay which will appeal to most Canadians is the recognition it takes of a serious human problem. Aside from any consideration of economic interests, Canada owes a duty to the unfortunates of Europe and should share its good things with as many as possible of these unfortunate people.
I agree wholeheartedly with that view; and to-night I should like to make reference to one specific phase of immigration policy which I believe the government should adopt.
I appeal to the minister to give first consideration to stateless or displaced persons who find themselves to-day in Europe. Regardless of racial origin, these groups of people, should, I believe, have priority over all others. Of course I understand that in the first place we should bring back the men of our armed forces and their families. But following these two group, the government, in my opinion, has a moral and a Christian obligation to these unfortunate people of Europe who to-day find themselves scattered in practically every country in the old land, without homes, without food, without shelter, and without hope. I want to make as strong a plea as I possibly can on behalf of these

Supply-Immigra tion
tormented and unfortunate people, who perhaps have during the war sacrificed much more for us then we would sacrifice for them.
May I point out that this group comprises the democratically-minded people who had to move on into western Europe when totalitarianism was advancing. I. find that in the Edmonton chamber of commerce report the fear is expressed that it may be impossible for us, or perhaps too late, to get some of these people to come to Canada. The report continues:
It is obvious therefore that, if we wish a national increment in population through immigration to Canada, the federal government, collaborating with the provincial governments and industry, labour and agriculture, must make plans at once before it becomes too late.
The Edmonton chamber of commerce, after studying this problem carefully, have come to the conclusion that it may not be so easy to get these people to come to Canada as we may think.
I should like to make one or two other references to the arguments that are being advanced by some government officials and other individuals against admitting people into Canada at this time. In the first place, they argue that there is no passenger accommodation on ships and that therefore this problem cannot be considered at the present time. In the second place, they argue that no immigration should be encouraged until our returned men are reestablished in peace-time occupations. I agree that that is the view which we should take. At the same time, however, I would point out that the immigrants who would come to Canada would not for the most part know the English language and therefore could not displace our returned men. In the third place-at least I gather this from some of the correspondence which I have received, as well as correspondence which has been handed to me by others-the government does not feel that immigration should be allowed until our economic system is adjusted. But, Mr. Chairman, some of these people in Europe will be dead by that time. They cannot wait until we adjust our economic system; and besides, the individuals who are interested in bringing these people to Canada are ready to guarantee and to provide a livelihood for their relatives. The fourth argument used is of course a weak one, that nothing can be done "at the present time". That argument does not answer any question; it is no argument. And the last argument that is used was that these people would have to present their passports before being allowed to come in.
May I point out that during this war hundreds of thousands of people were trying to
save their very lives and had no chance of saving or of obtaining passports. I was glad to find that the British government took the only logical and humanitarian stand on the question. In spite of our desire to rush through our estimates and finish this session,
I think I ought to put on the record an announcement which appeared in the Times of London, England, on November 14, 1945. The reason I wish to put it on the record is simply to show that the British isles, which are so crowded, where they have not even sufficient food for their own people and no housing accommodation, decided that anyone residing in Britain might bring in relatives, and not later on but now.
Perhaps I should not weary the committee by putting this on the record, but the essence of the point I wish to make is simply this. Despite the fact that they have no room for more immigration, that the returned men are not rehabilitated as yet, that their economic position is not stabilized, the British government is allowing these people to come in. I am happy to say that in spite of the fact that the government in Britain has changed recently, the people of Britain have not changed in their humanitarian attitude toward this problem.
I was disappointed that Canada was not the first nation to make that move. Canada should have been ithe country to make the announcement, to say. "We have these open spaces; we have natural wealth with which that of no other nation is comparable. Why, therefore, should we not welcome as many of these people as we can?" I know the argument i3 that there were no ships. But as the member for Spadina pointed out, our men will be brought back by the spring at the latest, and their families shortly after that. Surely it would take several months to issue permits of admission to these people. Why not undertake now to issue those permits and have them post-dated? The only request I make to-night on behalf of these displaced persons in particular is this-because the broader aspect of the immigration problem will be discussed at the next session, whether we desire an increase in our population-that we help these people by announcing that we are ready to accept a certain quota of them now and that we shall issue to them post-dated permits of admission. If this were done, those who are in Britain, or France, or in parts of Germany and elsewhere would know that there was something to look forward to. Surely we can do that.
May I make one or two other observations. I notice that in one of the orders in council passed in recent years there is a strict require-
Supply-Immigration

ment of medical inspection. In a general immigration policy I agree that proper health safeguards should be maintained, but I hold that it is not reasonable to demand robust health of those who have undergone the suffering, privation and hunger and all the hardships that these people have experienced. We cannot expect any high standard of health from these displaced persons. That is hardly the thing for us to do. What we should do is to try to save some of these lives. We must remember that many of these people find themselves where they are to-day because they fought the battle on the hattlefield. They are the ones who went through the privations and horrors of war, while we in Canada enjoyed perhaps the highest standard of living we ever had. There was not a single acre of land scorched in this country; there was not a single home bombed out at night; there was not a single family that did not have a roof over their heads; therefore I consider that we should consider this problem purely from the Christian and humanitarian viewpoint. I appeal to the minister and to the government to give most sympathetic consideration to the suggestions I have made.

I had intended to speak for some time on this subject, but it has been so ably covered by the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Hlynka) that I feel I can make my remarks very brief. I should like to support him in what he has said to-night and to add my word to the need for planning, the need for a committee on immigration), and to emphasize our moral duty to stateless and displaced persons.
I consider that our greatest need to-day is a committee on immigration. There are so many intricate problems coming up with regard to nationals of many countries that unless they earn be brought before a committee to be discussed privately and the difficulties ironed out, I feel that in the next session the minister will have a tremendous task before him. I think we are all aware of the problems and difficulties that are facing the government to-day with respect to immigration and the problem of dealing fairly with the nationals of many countries. We know there are transportation difficulties in repatriating our soldiers, war brides, and their children. We know there is a critical shortage of housing, an unemployment problem and many other problems. But we have such tremendous resources in this country that we can absorb a moderate number of people and discharge this moral duty within the next few years.
I am one who is most anxious to do everything I can to further that great work. I should like to make one reference to the

work of an eminent historian, Mr. Griffiths Taylor. I do not altogether share his opinion for in this work he analyses Canada's position and outlines the number of people who might be settled here. He says that Manitoba could support 63,000,000 people, that eastern Canada could support 96,000,000 people and that adjoining regions could support 30,000,000 people. That makes a total of 189,000,000. That is not my opinion but that of Mr. Griffiths Taylor, 'an eminent geographer and historian.

I can give the committee another figure *which may interest it. For the whole North American continent he estimates a total of 702 million; the eastern United States, 298 millions. That is based on natural resources; coal, iron, fertility, rainfall, electric power and many other things. It is an analytical treatise, not a work of fiction.
However, I shall not delay the committee any longer than to put on record a resolution recently passed in Toronto which shows how the citizens of that city feel toward the present situation in Europe. The first point is that the right of asylum should be granted to displaced persons in western Europe; second, that the displaced people should be provided with lodgings, food, clothing and. medical care for such time until a way can be found to reestablish them permanently; third, that every effort should be made to reestablish displaced people in a country where they can live out their lives peaceably without fear of want or persecution. These are the resolutions of one committee. I have also a special request from

one section of the community, which is in the form of a letter to the Prime Minister. It refers to the Polish people and says:
As the Prime Minister of a mighty and most respected nation, and as one in whose power lies the granting of our wish ... we beg you to admit into Canada discharged servicemen of the Polish forces who wish to settle here and give them the opportunity to love the freedom and heritage of a noble and democratic power, just as we value it beyond worldly expression.
These are just two quotations from the letters and resolutions which have come into my hands.
May I conclude my remarks with a word to the department. In my dealings with them I have been met with extreme courtesy and helpfulness. I know they have been tremendously overworked by the problems that have been thrust upon them. I am glad to see that there is some increase in their estimates to help- them deal with the problems that are before them. I hope that in the future able men will not be so closely bound by a rigid Immigration Act which gives us practically no power to select and very little opportunity to bring good and loyal fighting men and their families to this country. I have served with a number of these men to whom I am referring, namely, Polish airmen. I know the tremendous loyalty, courage and powers of endurance which they possess. I know they would be good citizens; I know it is the feeling of the men in the armed forces of this country that they would like to welcome them to Canada and to have them as citizens. In the past we have accepted new Canadians, as they are called in many communities, without any attempt to nationalize them. I know the Secretary of State will be interested in the suggestion that when we bring new people to this country we do not cast them on the mercy of a community or make it necessary for a few friends or relatives to care for them. When we bring them to this country we should bring them into a nationalization centre where they can learn something of our institutions and the growth of a democratic state, where they can learn to appreciate the way of life which we live, and learn to love our country as we love it.

What I wish to speak about now is not mass immigration, because we all agree that our first responsibility is to the men overseas. Until they are back and settled in jobs, and we know exactly what Canada's economic position will be, it would be very hard for anyone to say that we should open our doors wide and let everyone come in. I want to speak more specifically about the people who suffered most as a result of
Hitler's barbarism; that is, the Jewish people.
I do not believe any hon. member can speak with more feeling about this matter, because I was born in a city in Poland, and I know the exact spot where a million and a half Jews were murdered by the nazis; that is, at the Maidanek camp in Lublin. Therefore I feel much more strongly about this matter than most hon. members, who have only read about it.
The Ottawa Citizen of this evening, telling about the Nuernberg trial of the twenty-one top leaders of Hitler's gang, states that six million Jews were ruthlessly slaughtered in the nazi campaign of extermination, according to the figures of the German secret police. Some Jews saved themselves in almost miraculous ways. They, escaped from the camps; they hid their identity; they were saved by non-Jews. In these ways some of them managed to remain alive. They are not in the best of health; as a matter of fact they are very weak, having gone through hell, and I cannot find any more polite word to describe it. Some are' still kept in concentration camps in the American and British zones. The other day we heard Mrs. Lorna Wingate, the widow of General Orde Wingate of Wingate's raiders, who made a very strong plea on behalf of the Jewish people to about one hundred members of this house. She also spoke in the city of Toronto where, in referring to the Jews in camps in western Europe, she said:
These Jews are living ghosts . . . They have gone through hell and nave come out the other side. Their home is a concentration camp where the bones of their brothers and sisters lie buried in a few feet of earth. They are fenced in as they were when the Germans were their masters. Their food allotment is less than the Germans who stare at them from outside the fences
I am not asking that we bring to Canada all those left alive in Europe, but I am appealing particularly on behalf of those who have in this country relatives who are willing to bring them here and look after them, without taking a single job away from anyone. I have here some appeals coming from such people in western Europe. Here is a letter from one who was a lieutenant in the Polish army. He was taken prisoner by the Germans in 1939 and liberated by the Americans. His parents live in Montreal and are citizens of this country. He writes to them in English, as follows:
Six years captivity may achieve very, very much! I have got used to many things; above all to endure every injury, to submit to all decrees of fate, and to persevere in patience. But day goes after day, and the years are fleeting. . . . The most irritating and painful problem now is the open question-what to do, whither to go?

He concludes by appealing to his parents to bring him to Canada. A permit was issued to this man allowing him to come to this country in 1928, but now he is told that he may not come. He had a. wife and child in Warsaw. They are dead. He has no one but his parents and other relatives who are in Montreal, but he cannot come here because the department tells us that there are no ships. I insist, however, that Portuguese ships would bring these people h^re if their relatives were permitted to arrange passage for them. Here is a letter from a girl eighteen years old, written through the Red Cross. She says:
I was five years in a concentration camp in Auschwitz-
And Auschwitz camp, according to the evidence reported from Nuernberg to-day, is the place where a million and a half people were murdered.

and have nobody in the world only my uncle. I beg you very much for an answer.
Well, she can get no answer because under present conditions there is a strict ruling in effect even against these people who have lost their families in Europe and have relatives only in Canada. None of them ever helped Hitler; they were always his greatest opponents; they have suffered most at his hands; yet to-day they cannot come to this country.
I wish to make an appeal on their behalf. Even before the next session of this parliament something must be done to give a spark of hope to people who cannot think of returning to the places where their relatives lie dead' as a result of barbarous treatment and murder. Our humanity should be such that we would give these people an affirmative answer and say, "You can come to Canada. We will do at least this much to make up for the suffering you have gone through."

I wish to say just a few words on behalf of a specialized group of those who have suffered from the dislocation of Europe.
I believe some very fine ideas have been advanced to-night, but I also believe there are a few things which are quickly forgotten in connection with this whole situation. We have just finished a dreadful war. While that war was in progress we said to those people, "This is your war and ours, and it will be your victory and ours." Then the shooting stopped; the papers were signed, and we came to the parting of the wa3's. They went on to hunger, exposure and disease; we returned to warmth and prosperity. But I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this is our peace; this is our joint victory and our joint responsibility. We who are more prosperous now than we have ever been, because of war, cannot disown 
these brothers ini arms who gave their lives, their children, their homes and everything they had in the cause we supported. These people who joined underground movements and deliberately destroyed their bridges, their shipping, their railways, their factories and their resources, believed that when peace came we would restore these things which they so cheerfully sacrificed. We whose national income was tripled during the war now grudgingly vote them one per cent of it. I think our contribution to UNRRA is shamefully small; and I believe that the attitude we have adopted so far in regard to the victims of this struggle is unworthy of this great country.
One group deserves special consideration, and for a moment I am going to talk about the children of Europe. Recently I had the pleasure of talking to several persons who came a short time ago from that unhappy continent. They tell us that there are various groups who need to be sorted out, before we shall know exactly how many there are. Then there are the orphans of Europe, those whose parents died in concentration camps, in slave labour camps, and those children who have been orphaned because their parents were actively engaged in the underground movement. Those children have given everything.	.
Then there are the unhappy children who are the result of the dislocation of war. A very fine Quaker lady told us a week or so ago that in Norway, alone, there are thousands of children born of German fathers, who are considered to be a blot and a reproach. They are the unwanted children, the result of the invasion, and Norway now would like someone to take them off their hands. These are the unhappy by-products flowing from the dislocation and upheaval of war. We cannot ignore them. We who gained so much cannot say now that the war is over, "this is Canada; this is our country, and we have no further obligation." We cannot do that sort of tiling.
I am pleased that there are those in every group in the house who are prepared to rise in their places and say that they will not be a party to any action of that kind. The children of Europe to whom we could give shelter would not compete in our labour market, nor would they be a charge on the government. In a radio broadcast I delivered a few weeks ago I spoke to the people of my constituency, and the people in the surrounding area. This was a speech delivered in the "Report From Parliament Hill" series. In my broadcast I asked those people to write to me letting me know whether they knew German families who would take German children,

Supply-Immigration
Polish families who would take Polish children, or people from other European countries who had come to Canada, who are now Canadians and who would be willing to accept children from various parts of Europe. I was delighted with the response. I have received letters every day from people who are only too anxious to help, and who are waiting for us to open the doors so that these children may be let in. I have here a letter from a young . doctor and his wife, who is Scottish. They have a child of their own, and they ask now for a Polish child, because they say that the Polish people suffered more than any others.
Then, I have figures here to show what Great Britain has done. Let us remember that Great Britain has always been overcrowded, that it is one of the most heavily populated countries in the world, and that a third of her homes were either damaged or destroyed. But in the midst of scarcity, privation and overcrowding, this is what Britain did, as described in a speech by Mr. Anthony Eden in the British House of Commons in December, 1943:
As regards our own country since May, 1940, all of it a difficult period for us, we have taken some 60,000 non-British refugees and they are still coming in at the rate of about 800 a month. Great Britain is continuing to give 'accommodation to displaced persons.
As was stated recently by the hon. member for Vegreville, they are allowing non-British people who are now resident in Great Britain to accept their relatives, and to give them homes in that country. I hope we shall not wait for the next session of parliament to set up a committee. I hope that we who are so comfortable, so callous and so smug will open our hearts and begin to make preparations, so that when these children are sorted out and are made available we shall be in a position gladly to accept thousands of them. Our Canadian homes are 'waiting to take them in.

I wish to make only two or three remarks. It seems to me there are two ways of looking at this question of immigration. One, of course, is from the point of view of relieving the distressed in Europe, and the other way is that of looking at the-question from the point of view of benefiting Canada. I am not one who believes that merely by bringing in immigrants Canada automatically will be benefited. We have had a lesson of that in the past. If Canada is to benefit from bringing in more immigrants, then I feel that we shall have to make conditions in Canada such that the immigrants will be glad and willing to stay after they get here.
That cannot be said of the past. I have been in Canada since 1901. I do not know the number of people who have come here during that time-it would run into the millions, I suppose-but I do know that in the same time very nearly as many people have left Canada because they thought the United States and other countries offered greater opportunities.
Therefore it seems to me that apart altogether from the humanitarian point of view, if Canada is to benefit by having more immigrants, then we certainty shall have to see to it that after they get here they will be able to find opportunities and to maintain a standard of living which will induce them to stay here, and which will not encourage them to look abroad for somewhere else to go, as they have done in the past.

I .do not wish to speak at length, but this is a matter of great importance and I should like to say a few words about it.
I want it to be clear that in approaching this question of immigration I am not unmindful of the fact that Canadian service personnel and war brides should receive first priority in the matter of entrance to this country. We do not ignore that necessity.
However, when that situation has been relieved to the point where some people can be allowed into Canada, may I point out that there are a few things requiring consideration. There are immediate problems, "and long-range problems and policies.
The immediate problem seems to be that of finding ways and means of helping those millions of people in Europe who have been roaming up and down from one country to another, and who are classified as displaced and sometimes as stateless people.
About a week ago I attended a lecture in Ottawa addressed by Mr. Edward Cahill of Boston, Massachusetts. This gentleman was in Europe not long ago, and he had seen at first hand something of the problem of displaced persons. I am sure that any other hon. members who heard him must have felt much the same way as I did. Some of the experiences he described were sufficient to give one the creeps. Among other things he said that there were anywhere from 20,000,000 to 30,000,000 people in Europe to-day who could be classified as displaced. They find themselves in the position where they do not know how they are going to live through the winter. In fact, he predicted that unless something unforseen and almost miraculous is done there will be hundreds of thousands and perhaps several million who will not see the spring.
Supply-Immigration

He pointed out also that malnutrition has advanced so far that there are hundreds of thousands of people in Europe who, even though they are fed the best of food for the rest of the winter, will still die of starvation. I am told by my medical friends that when malnutrition reaches a certain stage it becomes a sort of disease which mere food will not cure. In other words, there are thousands of people who are already doomed to death.
What about those who can still be saved? I believe we should be able to receive a certain number of these displaced persons or refugees. I say that because of what other speakers have said about Great Britain. We have a lesson to learn there. If a country like Great Britain, which has suffered far beyond anything that we can imagine, is still able to extend her hand to her neighbours and welcome them, surely we in this country who are so well off in proportion should be able to do a great deal more.
Let us not be afraid of accepting refugees. There has been a great deal of speculation in this country about that question. Let me refer again to Great Britain. One reason why Britain became great is the fact that she was always tolerant and broad-minded when it came to political refugees. She has always been ready to open her doors and allow freedom of expression for those from other countries. The Flemish weavers and the Hugue-, nots and others brought new skills and a new outlook that helped to build Great Britain to what she is to-day. I believe there is room in Canada for new skills and new aptitudes and perhaps new points of view.
I wish to make this clear, because unfortunately I have been accused lately by certain people of advocating the bringing into this country of nazi collaborationists. Anyone who has heard what I have said in this chamber can say that is not true. Let me make it perfectly clear that I am not advocating and never have advocated the bringing into this country of nazi collaborationists. I am one of those who denounced Hitler and Mussolini publicly many years before the war, at a time when some of these accusers of mine thought they were pretty fine fellows. I wish to make it perfectly clear that I do not want nazi collaborators in this country. I make that statement definitely, emphatically and without reservation. I hope that will be clear enough.
I want to see' people in this country, regardless of where they come from or what their nationality is, who believe in the principles of democratic freedom. I believe we shall find among the refugees of Europe some of the best democrats in the world. The
rMr. Zaplitny.]
fact that they have found it necessary to become refugees, to get away from totalitarian rule, proves that they have the principles of democracy and freedom so deeply in their hearts that they were willing to suffer privation in order to preserve them. So much for the immediate problem.
Then a word as to the long-range policy. I should like to point out that there definitely is room for expansion in this country, and I should like to give a few figures to illustrate . what I mean. In 1851 there were in this country 2,312,919 people; in 1941 there were 11,506,665 people, an increase of about 9,000,-
000.	Of that number, over ,6,000,000 were immigrants. Roughly speaking, two-thirds of the increase between those two dates was made up of immigrants. I do not know what the target should 'be for the future; I do not know what we should aim at or what we want our population to be at any given date, but from those figures we can see that there is certainly room to carry on if we are to have an expansionist attitude in this country.
The attitude of labour and of the veterans on this question is quite clear. I wish to put that on the record, because it is important to make it clear that anything I may say to-night or at any time is not intended to clash with the views of organized labour. We in this group have always tried to look after the interests of labour. I should like to put on record the attitude of the Trades and Labour Congress and the Canadian Congress of Labour toward immigration. First, I should like to read a resolution adopted by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada at their 1944 convention, reading as follows:
Whereas there is a demand in some quarters for a softening of the restrictions on immigration to this country;
And whereas the war in Europe has created a terrific refugee problem in connection with the mass flight of hundreds of thousands of innocent victims of the nazis;
Therefore be it resolved

that Canada's Immigration Act be revised to make it possible for Canada to do her share in granting refuge to her full quota of refugees;
And be it further resolved-that a policy of accepting immigrants into this country be pursued so long as such policy in no way adversely affects living standards or the welfare of our present Canadian population.
The following is a resolution passed by the Canadian Congress of Labour ait its convention held in 1944:
Be it resolved that the Canadian Congress of Labour in convention assembled request the dominion government to institute a concrete plan of immigration during the post-war period, without any danger of displacement of present labour, and along the following plan:

(1)	The selection of immigrants whose personal training and qualifications will permit them to be used in the development of the sections of Canada that are not being fully utilized, as well as in new developments of industry for which they are fitted.
(2)	The acceptance of only those immigrants who are able to pass a reasonable health examination.
(3)	Every possible assistance to be given them in developing and maintaining a standard of living comparable to that existing in the dominion at the time of their arrival.
I should like to place on the- record the attitude of the veterans as outlined in the publication Canadian Veterans. This article reads:
One thing is certain:	that no intelligent
Canadian can possibly expect that the open spaces of this dominion are going to go unpopulated long in a world where people are starving for want of arable soil-a world in which all sections are neighbours within a day's journey of each other.
Sooner or later those spaces are going to be filled. It is up to us, just as soon as our veterans are settled, to eschew any dog-in-the-manger attitude that may exist, and to spread out arms 

judiciously-to immigration.
The attitude of those three organizations is fairly similar; they are in favour of an immigration and expansionist policy as long as proper safeguards are taken to make sure that the interests of organized labour and the discharged veterans are not affected. That is the attitude I am taking to-night and that is the attitude of our group.
I agree with what the hon. members for Spadina and Trinity said about the necessity of having a committee on immigration. I should like to add to what they said by suggesting that when this committee is set up it should receive advice from representatives of labour and agriculture, and from -the professional groups, so that it will receive the representations of all the different classifications and occupations in Canada.
I was interested in hearing what the hon. member for Wetaskiwin had to say about immigrants coming to Canada but not remainT ing here. That is true. I have figures here from the Canada Year Book which show that six out of ten persons who came to Canada as immigrants left for some other country, the greater part of them going to the United States. The reason for that is fairly obvious. If the people who come here cannot find what they are seeking; if they cannot find occupations that will give them a good standard of living, naturally they will go where they can find what they want. I believe that in that connection our immigration will be tied up with our economic system. If we adopt an economic system based on a policy of expansion, of making the greatest possible use of our natural resources, it will be possible for us not only to keep up a high standard of
living for our people at present in Canada but also to admit thousands more. If, on the other hand, we adopt a policy of contraction; that is, if we allow ourselves to drift back to the system -in the years of the dark thirties, then it will be a question not of immigration into this country, but of emigration to somewhere else.
'Mr. GAUTHIER (Portneuf) (Translation): Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief in the remarks I have to make. May I say, at the outset, that the note I shall strike to-night will not be in complete harmony with the concert you have just heard in support of immigration.
Some hon. members advocate a fairly massive immigration, others would favour a less extensive immigration, and others still merely want this country to look with compassion upon those who have most suffered in all countries of Europe.
I must state at once that if sometimes certain members of this house are compelled to take a stand that appears somewhat radical on some matters, they do not do so because they hold radical views but quite often in order to oppose a theory implying the promotion of various projects which are not in keeping with -our needs and especially with existing conditions.
As I said, if I am striking to-night a note which is not quite in harmony with those you have heard so far, it is not because I wish to ostracize any nation or race. Far from it. I have enough Christian feelings to sympathize with any people in their hardships, but my Canadian spirit is also sufficiently deep to prevent me from forgetting the plight, -if that word is not too strong-of my own country while commiserating with other unfortunate people.
It is true that in other countries hardships have been suffered, that children were massacred and that a number of men and women have spent months and years in concentration camps, but it is also true that Canada has done her share to alleviate all those hardships. It is true that hundreds of thousands of our soldiers have left Canada, whether in the air force, the army or the navy, in order to join in the fight against ideologies that were too wide-spread, not only in Europe but in many other countries, and which had become deeply-rooted in the minds of some people. It must be remembered, however, that Canada has sent overseas a large number of troops in addition to the billions which we have sent to the continent to help the people of those European countries. Further that we continue, through UNRRA, to help relieving the sufferings of those countries.

v	Supply-Immigration
I understand that some families may wish to adopt young children who have suffered while they were in Europe, but we must remember that in our own country there are children who also have suffered and who are still suffering; some fathers have left their families to go to war and they have not returned, and their children are now orphans. Others went overseas and have returned seriously wounded or crippled for life; thus, their families, although they may not be in dire need, cannot live in the comfort which they had the right to expect.
We must not forget that we are also faced with the problem of our returned men. I was a member of the committee on veterans' affairs, and I have seen members of all the groups in this house take part in all the discussions and study, in a practical and intelligent manner, the problem of the Canadian veterans. And until this problem has been settled, and as long as our law makers refer to repatriation, relief for our veterans, land settlement, there can be no thought of adopting an immigration policy which would but add to our difficult and urgent problems and would complicate conditions in our country.
Hence,. Mr. Chairman, even if I may appear somewhat radical-I have already been referred to as such, but this does not worry me-it is because I believe that any government, or any country whatsoever, must be possessed of a nationalist feeling, even if this word may shock some pf the hon. members present, and I mean that we must think of our own country first.
I do not think that anyone could say that Canada has been guilty of selfishness during the war. I do not think we should open our doors wide to immigration for we already have enough important, urgent and difficult problems to solve.
An hon. member has suggested a committee on immigration. I would like to be a member of it so as to make a thorough, intelligent and appropriate study of the matter.
Those who are here to-night and who have studied world history, know that it is impossible to prevent, in any part of the world, the migration of populations from one country to another. This fact is generally recognized. However, no member of a legislature, whoever he may be, whatever group he may belong to, whatever school of thought he may follow, may abstain from requesting the government he supports or opposes, to be very careful in the selection of immigrants. The immigration officers can never be too strict, for it is only after an immigrant has lived in his adopted country, that it is possible to judge him on his merits.

It may well be claimed, it is true, that the young refugees we may bring into our homes by thousands or hundreds of thousands, will not immediately become public charges. No immigrant, moving from one country to another is exempt, on his- entry into his adopted country, from the supervision pres-scribed by the law of the land and from a special attention on the part of the authorities; by this fact, he plays a part in the shaping of social measures which become ever more numerous and more important.
This is the reason why I rise to my feet to-night. It is not that I wish to sound a false note in this debate, not that I wish the people of Canada to believe that I am irremediably opposed to any immigration policy, but rather that I wish to point out, before we throw our doors wide open to immigration, that we should give some thought to our own interests and to the settlement of our domestic problems, for we must prevent the recurrence of extensive unemployment, which might indeed well prevail after the war.
I therefore hold the view that we should first think of our young children, of our incapacitated soldiers and veterans. Once their case is settled, there will be nothing to prevent us from surveying the situation and implementing a policy not of the open-door but of restricted immigration, insisting on the most careful selection of the immigrants which are to be allowed to enter our beautiful Canada.

The hon. member then asked: What was the basis upon which decisions were made as to who shall be entitled to war duties supplements and reclassifications. War duties supplements in my department are paid to those employees who have assumed substantially increased duties and responsibilities directly related to the war effort and to those who assumed the full duties of higher classified employees on military leave.
To arrive at the amount of the supplement, the department reassesses the position in the light of the additional duties, and the amount of the supplement recommended is the difference between the employee's existing salary and the minimum salary rate of the class to which reclassification would normally be made. The recommendation with ministerial concurrence is then submitted to treasury board.
In the Department of Transport, including air services, a total of 708 employees were granted war duties supplements. Forty-nine recommendations were not approved.
Reclassifications in the Department of Transport fall into the following two categories:
1.	Employees in classes of grade 1 or lower -office boys, clerks, typists, et cetera-when their names were reached on the civil service commission eligible lists as a result of competitive examinations, were recommended for reclassification to the next higher grade if their duties warranted same.
2.	Employees in divisions of the department designated as war units by treasury board. Units so designated are merchant seamen manning pool, controller of transport, and war-time construction division of air services branch. These new divisions were subject to constant and rapid expansion and, as from time to time employees assumed duties greatly in excess of their original classification, they were recommended for higher classification.
The hon. member for Peterborough West-asked a question about weeds in the Trent canal. The reply is that the department removes weeds in the main- channel, but not opposite'approaches to private docks.

May I just say one word with respect to the estimates of the Department of Transport. I do not think we shall have to ask for much in the way of information, but in view of the absence of some of our members I would suggest that the first item be allowed to stand.

There is one matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. It has to do with the port of Vancouver. As the minister knows, the port

is operated by the national harbours board. There seems to be some question in the city about the operation of the port. Of course it is on the Pacific and therefore presents problems quite different from those of the Atlantic ports. The suggestion is made that the interest on the bonds is too high. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I believe it is five per cent.
That is right,

Another suggestion is that arrangements could be made to have the bonds refunded locally at a much lower rate, so that the port would not be paying such a high rate of interest. It is also suggested that the capitalization is too high, and that the cargo rates which are levied, I believe, on all tonnage passing through the harbour are a drawback, at least at their present amount.
When these ports were taken over by the national harbours board some of us felt that there was a danger of getting too centralized control; that the ports would get away from the initiative and the great interest that would follow from some form of local supervision. I believe that we have now come to the time when the weaknesses in this centralized policy are beginning to appaar. I would remind the minister that in 1931-32 a survey was made of the ports of Canada by Sir Alexander Gibb. With regard to having some local share in the operation of the port Sir Alexander Gibb had this to say, which is found at page 31 of his report:
It is essential to avoid emasculating the local administration, since no centralized control can replace an efficient and active local administration, or the special knowledge and initiative of the local business community, both of which are vital to a port's prosperity. For this latter reason I strongly advocate a local advisory council.
So far as I am aware that recommendation was never carried out in any of the ports. I continue:
There are very many aspects of port working which such a council can properly care for, such as the representation of the interests of private wharf owners, of local merchants and distributors, of local consignees and exporters, of the labour view and of the attitude of boards of trade, chambers of commerce, corn exchanges and other such trade organizations in addition to shipping.
It serves very usefully to identify the community with the port; and to secure the support and interest of local members of parliament, the city council, or provincial government in schemes, and so anticipate and meet criticisms from any such quarters, or action that might be prejudicial to the port.
It is invaluable in exploring the possibilities of local markets, in carrying out advertisement and propaganda and in cooperation with interests likely to promote industrial develop-

Supply-Transport
ments. Finally, a local council provides a useful check on the tendency of more or less permanent officials to become stereotyped or arbitrary.
The port manager would be ex-officio chairman of the council, which would meet regularly and be consulted on all such matters as proposed developments, alterations in rates, important changes in operation. The members of the council should have the right of initiating discussions on matters of policy affecting the port, on any complaints raised by users of the port, and on questions of rates, charges, et cetera; but not on any purely executive matters, and they would have no executive duties or powers.
The advisory council's proceedings and recommendations would be submitted to the central authority, and they should have the right of direct access to the central authority, but not to any other department of government.
There was no point in raising any of these questions while the war was on, but we are now facing a period1 of expansion, a period when there must be more interest taken in our ports. The fact that Vancouver is a port is the greatest asset of that city. It is the main Canadian port on the Pacific. There will be an immense trade across to the orient and to Australia and New Zealand if proper policies are followed1. I suggest -that within the next few months consideration should be given to the question of whether or not the port of Vancouver, and perhaps the other ports in Canada, are being handled in the most efficient and modern way.
The national harbours board have done good work; they have a very difficult job. But I suggest that the time has come to look over the whole situation and to stream-line the operation of our great ports. Would it be possible to have an investigation made with regard to the port of Vancouver? I suggest that the minister should go out there at the first opportunity. He has not been west since his appointment. Perhaps he could do so between the end of this session and the opening of the next.

The hon. gentleman has raised four questions. I shall deal with them briefly. The first had ito do with the rate of interest- on the debenture debt. I am not prepared to disagree with him on the rate. I may tell him that the national harbours board is considering the revision of it. No decision has been arrived at, but as soon as it has been reached, it will be announced.
With reference to capitalization, that is another problem which is continually receiving the attention of the board. I am not in a position to make any announcement on that.
With reference to cargo rates, they are being studied at the moment, and they may or may not be revised in accordance with whether there is a reduction in the interest rate of the
debenture debt. Sometimes it is the policy of the board and of the government to refund a series of debentures which come due at a certain date by borrowing the money on certificates of indebtedness and reducing the rate. Whether or not that will be done I am not in a position to say.
With reference to more local share in the operation of the port, 1 should say to the hon. gentleman that in large part that is the work of the port manager. Generally speaking, the port manager is a man who is taken from the community. He knows the circumstances; he is in contact with boards of trade, chambers of commerce and city councils. He has a local knowledge of the situation, and the national harbours board works with him. I am not prepared to say that what is suggested in the Gibb report is not a better conclusion, but at the moment that is the policy of the board. As far as a visit to Vancouver is concerned, I shall be happy to make one at the first possible opportunity.

Mr. MACDONALD (Halifax); I had not thought we would come to the national harbours board until later, but inasmuch as the hon. member for Vancouver South has brought up the question of our national ports I .should like to say a few words. In the first place, I

would invite the minister to home to Halifax and see a great port. He has been there before, I know, but not since becoming Minister of Transport, I was in Vancouver two or three weeks ago, and I told the hon. member for Vancouver South that I was very much impressed with the facilities I found out there and also with the development at Esquimalt. Kecently in Halifax we had a visit from the chairman and another member of the national harbours board. The chairman had been there a few months previously, and at that time he told us that the work of the port of Halifax in war time had been outstanding and beyond the most optimistic hopes of the members of his board. He informed us that no less than 56,780 ships had entered and cleared the port during the war, which represented an average of twenty-six a day.
No doubt the members of the board have had their thoughts and1 energies directed to war activities, and for that reason during the war years very little was done in the way of modernizing or developing the port facilities at Halifax. This whole question was recently brought to the attention of the Canadian people when the owners of the Queen Elizabeth objected' to Halifax and, instead, sent the ship to New York. Their objection was that an element of danger existed in wintertime if a southeasterly gale developed while the ship was lying at her dock in the harbour. Captain Bissett, the master of the ship, is a highly qualified master mariner, familiar for many years with conditions in the port of Halifax. It is true that the Canadian government made strenuous efforts to have the Queen Elizabeth go to Halifax, but the owners decided to accept the views of her master. Of course she is an exceptional ship; exceptional in size and draft and also in the very large area necessarily exposed to the wind. The owners decided to follow the advice of their experts. But experts give opinions, while facts are facts. Sometimes experts are wrong, and it would be very difficult to convince the people of Halifax that the experts were right in this case. They would1 be inclined to agree with the officials of the Department of Transport, who expressed the opinion that Halifax was quite a safe port for the ship to enter and dock. However, the British ministry of transport decided to accept the decision of the owners, and this decision has, I think, served a useful purpose in bringing to the attention of the people of Canada the necessity of modernizing the facilities of [DOT]the port of Halifax, or perhaps I should say the necessity of creating the most modern facilities at that port, for I dloubt if to-day it is sufficient to modernize facilities which were developed there at a time when no one 
contemplated ships the size of the Queen Elizabeth. It is not a case of constructing a new breakwater or extending an existing breakwater. I do not attempt to say what should be done, but Halifax must be a port where the largest British ship can lie in safety, and where no marine expert will be able to question the adequacy of the facilities.
The situation to-day is that, apart altogether from any developments made necessary by the action of the owners of the Queen Elizabeth, many other facilities have to be provided in order that Halifax will be able to compete on even terms with the great Atlantic ports of the United States. A few moments ago the hon. member for Vancouver South mentioned the Gibb report. It is true that this report contained a recommendation that advisory committees be set up at the national ports, and that this recommendation was never implemented by the government. Twenty years ago we had a famous report made on maritime rights, the Duncan report. The commission headed by Sir Andrew Duncan recognized that the development of a port was as much a matter of mechanical and technical equipment as was the development of any. extensive manufacturing or industrial business; and in their report they recommended that port facilities at Halifax and Saint John should be developed on such a scale as to create channels through which trade could expand both winter and summer. They recognized that such developments were necessary if our maritime ports were to be able to compete on anything like equal terms with the ports of the United States.
I must say that central control of our national ports has not been wholly a success. One result of central management is that a national port such as Halifax is not able to go out after business in competition with another national port. That being so, I submit that it is the responsibility of the' board and the government to see that business is directed to our national ports in something like fair proportions.
There is another consideration that should be kept in mind. In the house we have supported and approved proposals that our government extend credit to allied nations to enable them to purchase food and commodities in this country. We cannot control the movement of foreign ships, but I submit that we can at least insist that all goods shipped out of Canada for the relief of allied nations, or goods purchased in this country on the credit of Canada should go to our Atlantic national ports.
I do not wish to take up further time this evening, because the committee is anxious

Supply-Transport
to finish the estimates. However I suggest that in respect of our national ports there are two considerations which should be kept in mind by the national harbours board and the government. One is that all Canadian products which are bound for Europe should be shipped in the wintertime, through our own Canadian ports, if -they can be taken care of by those ports. The second is that full use should be made of the facilities of our maritime national ports in the summertime as well as in the winter. The government has the means as well as the obligation to see that these suggestions are carried out and this transitional period is the time to resolve that it will be done and to plan accordingly.

Apart from the uneconomic condition of having these incomplete railways, and the complete absurdity of railways with gaps in the
centre of them, it becomes evident at this time of the year that when people in that country run into difficulties on account of accidents or ill health, and have to drive anywhere from forty to sixty miles to a railway, that the need for completion is most evident. Might I point out that I dealt with, this subject at some length when my estimates were under discussion some days ago, and I do not think it is necessary for me to repeat to-night what I said at that time, namely, that consideration was being given, and that a committee had been set up by the Canadian National Railways to review this situation. The hon. member for Halifax spoke about the difficulty in connection with the Queen Elizabeth. May I assure him that officers of the Department of Transport, as well as those of the national harbours board were strongly of the view that the Queen Elizabeth could dock safely at Halifax.
He, and the hon. member for Vancouver South, spoke about advisory committees. At present, if one wishes to go to Edmonton from Prince Albert, he has to go to Saskatoon, board the train there, and go through to Edmonton. I agree.

do not know if it comes under this item, but if the minister would hear it now I shall not take up his time on another occasion. I have before me copies of letters written to the minister by representatives of the British Colmbia seamen's union in regard to a large number of arrests of sailors on Park steamship boats on their arrival in Vancouver. I notice in one reply under date of November 6 the minister states that he has ordered an investigation to be made. Has that investigation been made and, if so, what is the result? Many of the sentences imposed have been severe, and the seamen's organization point to the fact that most of the arrests have been on ships with British masters, that very few have occurred on ships with Canadian masters. If the minister has any knowledge of that factor I should like to hear what he has to say. Before I sit down I wish to say that I cooperate with the hon. member for Vancouver South in his extension of an invitation to the minister to visit Vancouver.
I may be able to give the hon. member a reply in a few minutes.

There seems to be a general impression abroad, which may or may not be right, that since railway construction has ceased, the duties of the board of transport commissioners have been lessening rather than increasing. I confess that I am surprised at the size of the staff and at the increase, although it is slight in this case. I should like to have a brief answer as to whether the duties of this board are increasing or whether we have a situation where an organization has been built up when it had many duties to discharge and then just sticks at that level.

If the duties of the board of transport commissioners have lessened in any way it would be because of orders passed under the War Measures Act. Order 92 of the wartime prices and trade board has to do with rates and the like, and to some extent it has curtailed the activities of the board. On the other hand, the board's activities have increased in other ways. During the war years the board has dealt with all sorts of applications and complaints with reference to rates, but always of necessity subject to wartime orders and regulations. It has been working in close harmony and cooperation with the transport controller because of the ancillary powers which the transport controller had during the war years. It has had duties in connection with the regulation and supervision of the carriage of dangerous munitions and explosives, and it has had jurisdiction over

railways, canals, shipping, telegraphs and telephones just as it normally had. Ninety per cent of the applications and complaints are disposed of without hearings; the other ten per cent are dealt with by'hearings held in various parts of the country. While its activities may have been curtailed by the war orders, I think the duties of the board have been as important and as necessary in war time as they were in peace time.

I notice there is a director of traffic, two assistant directors of traffic and a director of operations. Would it be correct to infer that when the war-time controls come off their duties will lessen?

I would think their
duties will increase rather than lessen.
Is this the board to which would be presented the claims of the importers and mines in the Northwest Territories?
Yes.

Since this matter was brought up in the house, I, and perhaps the minister and other hon. members, have been swamped with communications from gold mines and importers in the Mackenzie river valley. They are looking to the board for relief from the outrageous freight rates now being inflicted on the people trying to build up that country. Everybody there writes in complaining bitterly of what they have been up against. I would recommend to the minister that he instruct the transport commissioners to investigate this matter speedily. According to the Yellowknife Blade they are organizing up there and threatening more or less to set up their own government, which will see to it that they get fair play which they feel they are not getting now. As the minister himself stated a while ago, there is a freight rate of $30 a ton on oil. That is an outrageous rate, and even $20 a ton would be too much. Do not delay with this matter. There is no use in raising these people to a pitch where they cannot be calmed down easily. Some effort should be made to see that they are relieved of this condition so that this country can get along.

That sum of money is broken down under administration, improvements, replacements and repairs, operation and maintenance. Under replacements and repairs there is the sum of 815,000 to be spent in the Northwest Territories and $4,000 to be spent in the Prince Rupert area; and under operation and maintenance, two other amounts, one for Prince Rupert, of $63,900, and the other in the Northwest Territories, of $7,388.
I must inform the minister, first, that Prince Rupert is on the Pacific ocean and perhaps is not less than 700, perhaps 800 miles west.
I mentioned also the Northwest Territories.

And secondly-I say this kindly; I am not finding any fault with the minister-the Northwest Territories start at parallel 60. One-half of the Slave river is south of parallel 60, South of Fort Smith, and the Athabaska river is wholly south of the Northwest Territories. I should like to know whereabouts in the Northwest Territories the minister has reference to. The item must refer to the Slave river north of parallel 60 and the Mackenzie river from northwest of 47696-223
Great Slave lake. Now, just where? I am sorry to be persistent, but I am swamped with letters from up there asking me please to try to do something for them. I want to help the minister; I do not want the people of that section of the country to come down on his head.
I cannot give the hon. gentleman the information now. I will try to get it in a moment or two.

Mr. Chairman, there is needed in my constituency an improvement which I have requested for a long time. When I was elected in 1938 the promise was made that a bridge spanning the Lachine canal would be replaced by a tunnel. The plans of that tunnel were even ready. The estimates had been prepared and they were voted for two years in succession, in 1938 and 1939. Then war came and the work was stopped. Now that the war is over, I hope that the government will bring relief to that population of over 100,000 who are trapped, as it were, and find it quite difficult on many occasions to cross the canal.
That bridge is the most difficult to cross of all those that span the Lachine canal, on account of the near-by locks.
When still at a distance of 300 or 400 feet boats signal for the opening of the bridge. The gates are then closed and traffic is quite often stopped for fifteen or twenty minutes. On one occasion, we even had to wait three or four days before being able to cross the bridge. It had been opened, but could not be closed because a boat had stopped alongside. Ice flows down in the canal from Lachine when the locks are opened. There is in the centre a pier that blocks the bridge, and the boat had stopped there. On that occasion we could not cross the bridge for three or four days.
It was because of those conditions that the government decided in 1938 to undertake that work. Mention has been made of another bridge, the Atwater bridge, where the traffic is, I admit, heavier than over our own bridge, but that bridge does not remain open as long as ours. There is no lock in the vicinity of the bridge; boats proceed at a good speed at that place and the traffic is not so congested as at Cote St. Paul.
I hope the minister will take all those facts into consideration.
We have even prepared a table showing the traffic on the bridge of Cote St. Paul. We have noted the number of vehicles, trucks, motor cars, pedestrians, bicycles which use that bridge. That was in 1938 and to-day the traffic is twice as heavy. That table shows the traffic from nine o'clock in the morning to

The construction of this tunnel would bring a great deal of relief to one-third of the population of Verdun who would use it. There are also a large number of vehicles coming from the south shore via Mercier bridge and St. Patrick street, which cross over this bridge, and which greatly increase traffic. The construction of this tunnel would greatly improve conditions and would put an end to the congestion which takes place at this spot.
I hope that some means will be found to carry out this work. Plans had been prepared and tenders were to be called for when war broke out. We were told: "It is impossible to undertake this work now on account of the war." The people have understood but now that the war is over the electors of my constituency are desirous of having this improvement carried out. I have here a letter which I forwarded to the minister last month. In order not to delay the debate, in view of the late hour, I am willing to place this letter on Hansard with the consent of the house.
Very well, go ahead.

This letter reads as
follows:
Ottawa, November 5, 1945. The Honourable Lionel Chevrier, P.C., K.U., M.P.,
Minister of Transport,
Ottawa.

My Dear Minister,
Re: Tunnel of C6te St. Paul, Lachine Canal, Que.
Plans for the construction of a tunnel under Lachine canal, between the locks and the C&te St. Paul bridge, were prepared and completed in 1939. As I stated in my letter of September 12 last, this bridge is the worst located of all those crossing Lachine canal, because of the locks which are only four or five hundred feet from the bridge. When ships are a thousand or fifteen hundred feet from the bridge, they whistle to have the bridge opened. The gates come down, the bridge opens and traffic stops; automobiles, trucks, motorcycles, bicycles and pedestrians are forced to wait on either side of the bridge for fifteen to twenty minutes and sometimes longer. Ships proceed very slowly and the same thing is repeated when they come out of the lock. Sometimes two ships meet near the lock and then traffic is at a standstill for half an hour. Frequently there are over 125 automobiles and other vehicles, as mentioned above, in addition to pedestrians, waiting to cross.
Attached please find the report of a traffic survey held in May, 1938, between eight in the morning and four in the afternoon. From four to six in the evening, it has been impossible to keep up the work, for during that period, there is a general confusion. It must not be forgotten that this survey was made in 1938 when unemployment was still extensive. You are aware that traffic has doubled in the course of the last six years.
On each side of this bridge, there are two permanent railway lines, that of the C.N.R., on the north, and that of the C.P.R., on the south. At this point, the Canadian Pacific has a large yard, starting at Church street, which runs from the entrance to St. Paul bridge in an easterly direction. East of the bridge are the switches over which both passenger and freight trains are made up and switched to the various sidings. Every time a train is transferred from one siding to another, the traffic is stopped on the bridge, a condition which prevails through the whole year.
Moreover, although I cannot be sure of the year, but it was in the fall of either 1935 ot 1936, early in December, the bridge was completely closed to traffic for a period of four days. The ice that had jammed under the bridge prevented the passage of ships, six or seven of them being moored in the vicinity. Tugboats worked for three days, during which the bridge was open to traffic for only a few minutes. After all the ships had gone through, the ice was driven against the locks. We are threatened .vith the same condition each fall when the cold weather sets in and the ice begins to drift; then the bridge often remains open for half hours and sometimes longer, the ships stop facing the bridge and they have to be towed away.
The city of Montreal, as agreed, is still willing to give away the land necessary for the building of the tunnel.
I am convinced fifty per cent of the people of Verdun will be benefited by such a tunnel. Even a tramway 'ine uses the bridge in its circuit from Verdun to the city. Another line goes through to Ville Emard.
At the last elections, Cote St. Paul and Ville Emard had 19,000 voters; if you multiply that number by four, representing the average family, you have a total population of 76,000. There is more: the traffic for Ville LaSalle, at the exit

Supply-Transport
of Mercier bridge, is still routed by C6te St. Paul bridge, which increases congestion to a greater degree and is a further argument for the building of the tunnel which has been under consideration for about thirty years.
I could supply other detail, but I know you have them in your files concerning the proposed tunnel. As projects have been promised for the post-war period, I feel that none would be more essential than the building of the C6te St. Paul tunnel.
I will see my two colleagues of the House of Commons who are interested in the building of the COte St. Paul tunnel and I am sure they will support my request by letters they will send you.
I hope, dear sir, that you will give my request the best possible consideration and that a favourable decision on this matter will be taken before the end of the present session.
Your devoted servant,
J. A. Bonnier,
Member of parliament for Montreal-St. Henry.
N.B. This tunnel was promised in 1938 and part of the money required was voted during the session of that year and re-voted in 1939.
