Is the minister prepared now to make a statement in regard to the Canso causeway or bridge, and the improvement of the grades and alignment on the railway? I will not discuss the matter at length because it was dealt with fairly fully at a previous sitting. The minister said that he was not prepared to answer at that time but would do so later in the session. If it is convenient to him I should like to have the statement now.

Before I reply to the
hon. gentleman, there are two or three questions which I wish to answer. The hon member for Vancouver East asked a question about the arrest of sailors on certain Park steamships in Vancouver. He said that most of the ships had British masters. I am informed that the men were charged under the Canada Shipping Act with offences against certain sections of the act having to do with refusal of duty and other serious breaches of discipline. The nationality of the captain had absolutely nothing to do with the charges that were laid. The seamen were members of the Westbank Park, Bridgeland Park and Cromwell Park. So far as the sentences are concerned, they would not be under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport. They are subject, I presume, to the ordinary jurisdiction of the magistrate or the police court that tried them, and I would have nothing to do with that.
With regard to the question asked by the hon. member for Davenport, there are two amounts in the estimates covering expenditures for the Northwest Territories: $22,388 in the 47696-223i
main estimates and $29,700 in the supplement-aries all having to do with aids to navigation in that area. I have the details, but they are lengthy.

Do they pertain to
dredging?

Transport has absolutely nothing to do with dredging; that comes under Public Works. We provide the funds for aids to navigation, buoys and assistance to navigation, but we do not deepen or dredge the channel. I have no objection to giving the details but. as I say, they are lengthy.
It is only a small amount in any event and it pertains to lights or buoys in the river.

It pertains to lights,
channel buoys, flag markers, bell buoys and shore beacons and it concerns those in Great Bear lake, Mackenzie delta, east channel and Port Brabant, in the Mackenzie river, and in lake Athabaska and Great Slave lake. There is also part of the estimate that has to do with the purchase of a buoy boat at Fort Smith.

I may inform the minister that these items do not amount to one, two or three as far as improvements are concerned. All the things he has mentioned are used every year. Every year they have to have buoys in the river and I have seen them myself.

There is far more in
the estimates this year than in 1944.

Does the minister understand the significance of the items he has mentioned? You could not go down the river without the buoys and markers. I know what they are. But is there anything in the item for the improvement of the channel in the rivers?

No. As I have told
the hon. gentleman, the improvement of the channel is a matter for the public works department. Transport has nothing to do with it. This department deals with aids to navigation, and this money is spent for betterments in connection with those aids.

Then I suppose the only thing is to ask at the next session of parliament to have these two departments put together. It does not sound feasible that the Department of Transport is unable to recommend to the Department of Public Works what has to be done. What does the Department of Transport do? The Department of Public Works will have to wake up; in fact both departments will have to wake up. Let
Supply-Transport

me read to the minister something from the Yellowknife Blade of November 20, written by John Murray McMeekan, a writer who is going to be heard from:
Ottawa Fiddles. We, in the Northwest Territories in the Yellowknife district, . . . and scattered throughout the district of Mackenzie and through all that vast imperial domain of more than a million square miles in extent which lies north of the provinces

That is, north of the 60th parallel, which is the northern boundary of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
-are in a state of suppression comparable to that which aroused the fighting ire of the colonists of North America.
I can tell the minister that there are ten to twelve thousand) people in that country, including vigorous young men who will not stand for the neglect that is going on there. They demand rapid transit. The Minister of Transport should see that they get it. I give him my own kindly and humble advice. I say to him:	As Minister of Transport, look into
this matter and see to it that, whatever the department does, these men get a square deal in the matter of transportation.

The hon. member for
Cumberland asked a question with regard to Canso, and I would preface my reply with this statement. In the estimate which is given here, any amount of money given is only an estimate, because the plans and the surveys are not yet complete and will not be complete for some time. Following discussion in the reconstruction committee of the House of Commons in 1944, the Minister of Reconstruction and the Premier of Nova Scotia arranged for an investigation of the existing situation. Mr. D. W. McLachlan, engineer of design and capital construction of my department, and Mr. L. H. Wheaton, engineer of the Department of Highways of Nova Scotia, were appointed to investigate and report on the same.
This report will not be completed until next year, one difficulty being inability to make a satisfactory arrangement with any contractor to undertake the work of borings in the strait of Canso. It is a difficult and expensive job, the water being 160 feet deep. A contractor has now been secured, but the work cannot be done until next spring.
I would have preferred not to make any pronouncement in the matter until the engineer's reports are in and the economic factors have been considered but, in view of the interest taken, I will make the following general statement as to the present situation based on the facts already developed.

The present Canso ferry is far from adequate, and the grades on the railway lines between Truro and Mulgrave are severe, while those on the line between Tupper and Sydney are fair.
Four solutions of the problem have presented themselves and we are developing accurate plans and estimates of these proposals:
1.	Bridge. The building of a low grade railway line from Sunnybrae to connect with the Antigonish-Mulgrave line, relocation of part of the Mulgrave line around the north coast from Lynwood and a bridge across the straits of Canso. Preliminary estimated cost, $26,000,000.
2.	Causeway and lock. Build a low grade railway line from Sunnybrae to connect with the Antigonish-Mulgrave line, relocate part of the Mulgrave line around the north coast from Lynwood to Archie Cove on the gut of Canso and build a causeway across the strait of Canso. Preliminary estimated cost, $19,000,000.
3.	New ferry. Build the same low grade railway line from Sunnybrae and relocate the Mulgrave line around the north coast to cape Porcupine on the gut of Canso, a tunnel between that point and Keaton point and establish new ferry terminals in that locality and build a large modern car ferry; also a corresponding new terminal on the opposite side of the strait. Preliminary estimated cost $10,000,000.
4.	Complete the Sunnybrae-Guysboro line and extend it around the south coast to Steep Creek on the strait of Canso, with a new terminal at Steep Creek and one on the opposite north shore. Preliminary estimated cost, $12,000,000.
The Department of Transport and the government are prepared to do anything within reason in the area. It realizes that something must be done both with reference to the railway and to the crossing. I have mentioned four possibilities. Before the department has complete data on these proposals, it is impossible to say which one will be adopted. All I can say at the moment is that whichever one of these is found by the engineers of the department to be economically sound will be recommended to the government.
What is meant by "preliminary estimates"? How are they made up? Are they casual guesses, or are they based upon some calculation as to the quantities, and so on?

They are not guesses; rather they are based on quantities estimated by the engineers. These preliminary estimates were made by the engineer of design and

Supply-Transport
capital construction of the department in conjunction with the engineer of the department of highways of Nova Scotia.

The minister said that the engineers are still making surveys for estimates and that they will not be completed until next year. Will they be available early in 1946? I understand that they have been working on it for some considerable time.
It is impossible to get a complete report until the borings in the strait have been made; and I am informed that it cannot be done at this time of the year.
What are they boring for?
To find out what the bottom is like, whether clay, sand or rock.
Do they propose to put piers on either side of the strait?
That would depend, of course, on the project that would be adopted; if it were a bridge or a causeway, yes.
A bridge would require piers?
Yes.
Does the minister know the depth of the water?
Yes, 200 feet deep, and the tide-
Near the shore?
No; it is 200 feet deep in about the middle of the gut.
That would have nothing to do with the bridge. What is it near the shore?
It is 100 feet near the shore, and in the gut the tide runs at five knots an hour.

In other words, if a pier were erected on each side of the strait, as is done for the Quebec bridge, it would be 100 feet deep. That is not out of the way, as long as the pier rests on a solid base. Is it a rock foundation?

That is what we do not know as yet. So far as the Quebec bridge is concerned, I am informed by the engineers that it would be impossible to build a structure of the nature of the Quebec bridge in the gut of Canso.

speechtext:
During the war a munitions ship caught fire and was sunk by shell fire in Halifax harbour. The following
year the cargo was removed, but the vessel herself is still lying in navigable waters, practically in mid-channel and is now a menace to navigation, particularly during storms when vessels may drag their anchors. She is a submerged wreck and her position is marked by two wreck buoys. The wreck should be removed because it is lying in good anchorage ground and, if damage to another ship were occasioned, it might prejudicially affect the port. I would ask the minister to have the proper officials of his department look into this matter.

Is my hon. friend referring to the Trongatel
Mr. MACDONALD (Halifax); Yes.
That matter is being investigated at the moment.

A situation
similar to that mentioned by the minister obtained in Tasmania, which is at the lower tip of Australia. Perhaps the tide does not run at five knots an hour there, but there is a strong tide. I cannot say as to the distance of the transverse down there. The minister is considering four points of view. In Tasmania they found a depth of water of 130 feet at the shoreline. The centre of the gap which had to be transversed was a mile and a quarter. The depth ran beyond 200 feet, and it was necessary to transverse this area. The estimate which the minister gave strikes me as being extremely high. In the particular area to which I am referring they gave up the project, but a young Tasmanian engineer conceived the idea of building large concrete pontoons and floating them into position. That obviated the necessity of putting a bridge structure down to that great depth They floated those pontoons into position against the current. The convex side of the pontoon was placed against the tide, and when the tide turned it held them in position. Then, by means of extremely heavy steel cables some eight inches in diameter and a mile and a quarter long, they floated these pontoons into position. Recesses were put in the top and bottom of these pontoons and on either side. By this means they constructed a structure at about one-fifth of the original cost. Even if Lloyds of London would not underwrite the structure in regard to the hazards it might undergo, the state of Tasmania took the responsibility and the structure has been completed. It is in use now, and has met with great success. The area which has to be traversed by navigation as well was overcome by taking the shallowest end in the 100 feet and putting in a lift bridge, which
Supply-Transport

permitted navigation to go back and forth. Perhaps it is my duty to mention this, although no doubt the engineers of the department know of it since it is one of the world's great achievements. I should like this on record for the consideration of the department, in view of the fact that millions are included in these estimates and spent just like so much water. Frankly, this is an extremely expensive chore that has to be undertaken by the department.

I am not sure whether the question I wish to ask comes under this particular item, but I have looked rather carefully through the estimates of the Department of Transport as well as those of the Department of Public Works, and I do not see any reference at all to money being expended for the removal of Ripple Rock.
That comes under Public Works.
And it can still be dealt with?
Yes.

I had intended to speak this evening on the advantages that would be derived from the construction of a canal across the isthmus of Chignecto connecting Northumberland strait with the bay of Fundy, but in view of the lateness of the hour and the amount of work still before the house I will reserve my remarks for another occasion. However, I should like to ask the minister if any consideration has been given by the government to the construction of this canal, whether any investigations are being made and any reports have been prepared.

No investigation has been made by my department other than that referred to in the report of the Chignecto :anal commission in July, 1931. The gist of that report can be summarized briefly in this quotation from it:
Having regard to transportation facilities already available in the maritime area as a whole, we cannot see where any interest would suffer were the Chignecto canal project to be permitted to stand in abeyance until it can be further examined in the light of future developments in Canada's economic situation.
Since that time it has not been further examined.
May I ask the minister what he has been reading from?
I have been reading from the report of the Chignecto canal commission dated July, 1931, set up by order in council P.C. 1686.

The minister stated that no investigations were being conducted by his department ait the present time. I would ask him to give the matter further consideration, and to have further investigations made. I believe further study should be given this important proposal.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
359. Marine service steamers, including icebreakers-maintenance, operation and repairs, $1,648,500.

I should like to direct two questions to the minister in connection with this item, since I see it deals with icebreakers. Will it be the intention of the department to maintain an icebreaker in future for use at Port Churchill, with a view to extending the shipping season there? I have a letter from several residents of Churchill in which they stated that the ocean-going tug the Ocean Eagle, which was originally built for use in Churchill harbour, was removed during the war and 'taken to the east coast. I understand that insurance rates are dependent upon the presence of the tug at the port. Will the minister do what he can in the near future to have that tug returned to Churchill? I do not wish to discuss the item further, because I understand that most of the money has already been spent.
I am informed that there is an icebreaker which goes to Hudson bay every season to open navigation. Then, so far as the tug is concerned, any ship entering the harbour is provided with a tug.
Where does the icebreaker come from?
It is the N.B. McLean. It comes from Quebec, and the east coast.
Is the ferry system between Borden and Tormentine included in this vote? Does this include the expense of operating an icebreaking steamer between those points?
No; there is a special vote for that.
Is it the intention of the present government to run the water up-hill from Newmarket to lake Ontario.

I read1 the other day where one of our ships had been equipped with radar. W'hat is contemplated by the department in this connection? How will radar assist in meeting the problems which arise in connection with navigation, for the avoidance of ice, and so on. This would have
a considerable bearing on a route such as the Hudson bay route, or on navigation in the strait of Belle Isle.

We are experimenting with radar on departmental ships at the present time. We have that equipment on the Grenville, one of the supply vessels which operate in the St. Lawrence. That is the only departmental ship equipped with radar at the present time. However, we are continuing our experiments, and they have been most satisfactory. I am also informed that when the McLean goes to Hudson bay next year she will be equipped with radar.

I understand that along the Hudson bay route the department is establishing several aids to navigation. Is it the intention to place landJbased radar at some of those points for the direction of ships?
No.

SCO. Construction, maintenance and supervision of aids to navigation, including salaries and allowances to lightkeepers, $2,043,400.

I received a telegram to-day respecting the light at Downing reef on Lake Winnipeg. What does the minister propose to do about this matter? Is it to be repaired and reestablished? I understand it has been demolished, and the people are anxious about it.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
365. Life saving service, including reward# for saving life, $44,250.

Perhaps on this item I might also speak respecting the subject matter in item 369, because there seems to be some relation between the two. Hon. members will recall the tragedy which took place last summer when fire broke out on one of the
Supply-[DOT]Transport

passenger steamers, one of the luxury vessels on lake Huron. I would refer particularly to life saving service, and to the inspection which would be covered by item 360.
In this connection may I put this observation on record? Since the advent of war very little has been done to keep this equipment in first-class condition. Some ten years ago it was my privilege to discuss this matter in the house, and to point out that there were not nearly enough safety appliances, especially on our passenger steamers on the great lakes, right from the Saguenay and the St. Lawrence through to Fort William. I repeat that tonight.
The advent of war in the meantime has not helped the situation. I note that in the coming year we are to spend $248,410 for steamship inspection, and that we are spending something more than $44,000 for life saving services. It will be my hope that with the two votes the department will realize that it has a tremendous responsibility to carry out life saving services and the inspection of craft that are dilapidated and old, and some of which are unseaworthy, and which will be expected to cater to the tremendous traffic we may expect to have in the coming year from those who will be seeking pleasure. Many people will have money to spend, which in days gone by they did not have. They will be crowding these out-moded services operating on the great lakes, from the mouth of the St. Lawrence right through the system.
It would well behoove the minister to advise the officials of his department who are charged with responsibility for these inspection services to see to it that when they accept in the coming year almost a quarter of a million dollars they do a job, even if it becomes necessary to restrict travel on unseaworthy craft, which will be catering to the trade in the next year.
Please, do not let us have more tragedies on our great lakes. Tell your inspectors, and those charged with the responsibility to carry out their duties in this day and generation when so many of our Canadian citizens are anxious to enjoy themselves and, if necessary, to spend large amounts of money in doing so.
Does the department still give medals for life saving? They used to give watches, too.
We do give awards. Sometimes they are made in cash, and sometimes medals are given.
Have any been given in recent years? Is the practice still current?
Yes, I have a list here.

The practice is still
current.

The committee on external affairs made a study of this convention and submitted certain recommendations for an increase in the number of tackle inspectors and an improvement- in their remuneration. Will there be anything in the supplementary estimates for that, because I notice there is provision for only four tackle inspectors at a remuneration of $1,440 a year? We were told in the committee that there were only two in British Columbia, one at Vancouver and one at Port Alberni. There is a sizable port at Prince Rupert, another at New Westminster and another at Victoria. How are ships coming into those ports to be inspected? These estimates were
prepared many months ago, and there could not possibly be any provision for additional inspectors of tackle, resulting from the signing of the convention, nor could there be such provision in the supplementary estimates which were prepared some weeks ago before the committee reported. ance they must go through the department, and it takes some time to prepare them in the department.

Has any consideration
been given to the completion of the railroad between Mankota and Valmarie on the Canadian Pacific? There is a gap here of about thirty-seven miles. I understand that resolutions and petitions have been sent to the minister in connection with this matter by R.M.'s 18. 45, 46 and 72 and the villages of Climax, Orkney, Masefield and Valmarie. I wrote to the minister in connection with this, but I have not had a reply.

I have received the
petitions, and I shall be glad to give my hon. friend a reply in due course.
Railway service-
375.	Hudson Bay railway-To provide for the difference between the expenditures for operation and maintenance, and revenue accruing from operations during the year ending March 31, 1946, not exceeding $500,900.

I notice that the expenditures to provide for the deficits on the operation of the Hudson Bay railway are increased in this
year's estimates by about $192,000. That might be accounted for in one of two ways; either the amount of the revenue is less, or the services have been considerably increased.
I should like to have a statement as to the present status of the service being given during the current year. I notice that the figures on page Z-25 of the public accounts of last year show the operating expenditures for 1943-44 as SL00S.025, and the operating revenues as 8660,000. giving a deficit of $347,872. The present deficit is considerably higher.

The manager of the railway appeared before the railways and shipping committee and gave evidence for some considerable time. The operating expenses for 1944-45 are $811,169.14; the revenue was $246,229.12, giving a net operating deficit of $564,940.02 as compared with $347,872.90. I have not the details here and I hesitate to go into it more fully. The manager gave these at great length before the committee, and I doubt whether this committee will want me to go over the matter again.
I had not read the report of the committee, but I was interested in knowing why there was an increased deficit.
Could this item stand until to-morrow? It is twelve o'clock.

REFERENCE TO REPORT IN TORONTO "DAILY STAR"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise on a question of privilege. Quite by chance I came into possession of a copy of the Toronto Daily Star, which reports this morning's proceedings with the following headlines:
Takes house five minutes to pass $2,000 M.P.
raise.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is symptomatic of the general distortion practised by this newspaper.

maintopic: REFERENCE TO REPORT IN TORONTO "DAILY STAR"
speechtext:
Oh, that is a good newspaper.

Exercise Musk-Ox

maintopic: REFERENCE TO REPORT IN TORONTO "DAILY STAR"
speechtext: I hope the Secretary of State was in the house this morning.

maintopic: REFERENCE TO REPORT IN TORONTO "DAILY STAR"
speechtext: The Secretary of State is always in the house.

maintopic: REFERENCE TO REPORT IN TORONTO "DAILY STAR"
speechtext: I am delighted. Then he must have been listening to his leader, or perhaps he did not? The question of privilege I wish to raise is that the debate took the entire morning sitting of this house, not the five minutes as distorted by this newspaper, which seems to be jointly owned by Hearst and Stalin.

maintopic: REFERENCE TO REPORT IN TORONTO "DAILY STAR"
